title: Forces we meet every day: reading the pushes and pulls on a still book, a falling cone and your own arm

summary.text: A book lies on a table and does not move. Is any force acting on it? In this lesson you learn to read the forces on everyday things, from the pull of gravity to the pull of your own muscles. You drop paper cones to find out what happens when the push of the air grows to match the pull of the Earth. Then you look underneath, and find that these many forces come down to very few, and that nobody can yet say what a force finally is.
summary.art: A book resting on a table with one arrow pointing down from its centre and an equal arrow pointing up from the table, and a child looking puzzled beside it.

intro.hook: Hold a school bag out in front of you with a straight arm and keep it perfectly still for one minute. Nothing is moving. So why is your arm getting tired?
intro.text: Your arm tires because your muscles are pulling upward the whole time. The Earth is pulling the bag down with a force. Your arm must pull up with an equal force, second after second, just to keep the bag where it is. So a thing that is not moving can still have strong forces on it. Today you will learn to find those forces, on a bag, a book, a kite and a fish, by asking two questions about each thing.
intro.art: A child holding a school bag at arm's length, with a down arrow on the bag and an up arrow along the arm.

outcomes: I can find the forces on an everyday thing by asking what touches it and what pulls it from a distance.
I can name gravity, support force, friction, tension, air resistance, upthrust, magnetic force and muscle force, and give an everyday example of each.
I can explain why a thing at rest, or moving at a steady speed, has balanced forces on it.
I can draw a labelled arrow for every push and pull on a book, a bucket or a kite.
I can explain why a falling paper cone stops speeding up.
I can say how a muscle makes a pull, and why a muscle often pulls harder than the load weighs.
I can say which everyday forces are, underneath, the same electric and magnetic force, and what is still not known about gravity.

explanations.concept: To read the forces on a thing, ask two questions
explanations.definition: The forces on an object come from whatever touches it and from a few things that can pull or push it without touching.
explanations.description: A force is a push or a pull. Several forces usually act on one thing at the same moment. To find them all, pick one thing and ask two questions. First: what is touching it? Each thing that touches can push or pull. Second: what is pulling or pushing it from a distance? In daily life the answer to the second question is nearly always the Earth, through gravity, and sometimes a magnet. Take a school bag hanging on a hook. The hook touches the bag and pulls up. The air touches the bag and hardly pushes at all. The Earth pulls the bag down from a distance. That gives two forces that matter.
examples: A dosa on a tawa: the tawa touches the dosa and pushes up. The Earth pulls the dosa down.
A ceiling fan: the rod touches the fan and pulls up. The Earth pulls down.
A steel pin under a magnet: the magnet pulls up from a distance, and the Earth pulls down from a distance. Nothing touches the pin for a moment as it jumps.
explanations.one_view: This is a working method used by every physics student and engineer, and it carries no dispute.
explanations.art: A school bag on a wall hook, circled, with two question bubbles: 'What touches it?' pointing to the hook and 'What pulls from far?' pointing down to the ground.
explanations.context: This card gives the two questions that the rest of the lesson uses to find forces.

explanations.concept: Gravity pulls on everything, all the time, towards the centre of the Earth
explanations.definition: Gravity is the pull that the Earth has on every object. The size of this pull on an object is called its weight, and it is measured in newtons.
explanations.description: The Earth pulls on you when you fall. The Earth also pulls on you just as hard when you sit, when you sleep and when you jump upward. Gravity never switches off. The pull on a one-kilogram bag of sugar is about 10 newtons. The newton is the unit of force. A child of 30 kilograms is pulled down with roughly 300 newtons. 'Down' means towards the centre of the Earth. So 'down' in Chennai and 'down' in Mexico point in nearly opposite directions. Gravity also works both ways. While the Earth pulls you with 300 newtons, you pull the Earth with 300 newtons. The Earth is so massive that your pull does not move it by any amount we could notice.
examples: A ball thrown up is pulled down the whole time, even on the way up. That is why it slows.
A mango on a branch is pulled down for months before the stalk gives way.
On the Moon the pull is about one-sixth as strong, so a 30 kilogram child would weigh about 50 newtons there.
explanations.one_view: How strongly gravity pulls, and in which direction, is measured and agreed. What gravity is and why it pulls is a different matter, taken up in a later card.
explanations.art: A round Earth with small figures standing in India, Mexico and at the South Pole, each with an arrow from their feet pointing to the centre.
explanations.context: This card treats gravity as the one everyday force that is always present, and gives its size in newtons.

explanations.concept: Astronauts float because they are falling, and gravity is still pulling them
explanations.definition: In a spacecraft going round the Earth, gravity is almost as strong as on the ground. The crew feel weightless because they and the craft are falling together.
explanations.description: People often say there is no gravity in space. That is not so. The International Space Station flies about 400 kilometres above the ground. Up there the Earth's pull is still about nine-tenths as strong as in your room. So why do astronauts float? Because the station is falling. It also moves sideways at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. That is so fast that as it falls, the round Earth curves away beneath it. It keeps falling and keeps missing the ground. The astronauts fall along with the station, so the floor never pushes up on their feet. What you feel as your weight is that push from the floor.
examples: In a lift that starts downward quickly, you feel lighter for a moment, because the floor pushes up on you a little less.
At the top of a jump on a trampoline, nothing pushes on you, and for a moment you feel weightless.
Rakesh Sharma in 1984, Sunita Williams on several flights, and Shubhanshu Shukla in 2025 all floated inside spacecraft. Gravity was holding those craft in their paths round the Earth.
explanations.one_view: The strength of gravity at that height and the speed of the station are measured, and every space agency flies by them.
explanations.art: The Earth with a space station on a circular path, a dotted line showing it falling and the ground curving away, and an astronaut floating inside.
explanations.context: This card corrects the common idea that there is no gravity in space.

explanations.concept: A table pushes up: the support force
explanations.definition: The support force is the push that a surface gives to anything pressing on it. It acts straight out from the surface.
explanations.description: Put a book on a table. The Earth pulls the book down with about 5 newtons. The book stays still. So something must push up on the book with 5 newtons. Only the table is touching the book. The table is pushing. How can a table push? When the book lands, the table top is squashed by a tiny amount, far too small to see. A squashed thing pushes back, as a mattress does when you sit on it. The table is like a very stiff mattress. Put a heavier book down, and the table is squashed a little more and pushes back harder. The table always gives exactly the push that is needed, until it breaks.
examples: Lay a metre ruler across two piles of books and put a tumbler in the middle. You can see the ruler bend. A table does the same, only far less.
A bathroom scale does not measure the pull of the Earth on you. The scale measures how hard its own top is pushing up on your feet.
Lean on a wall. The wall pushes sideways on your shoulder, or you would fall through.
explanations.one_view: The tiny bending of a loaded surface has been measured with fine instruments, and the support force is part of every engineer's sums.
explanations.art: A book on a table with the table top shown dented by an exaggerated amount under the book, like a mattress, and an arrow pushing up.
explanations.context: This card pushes against the idea that only living or moving things can push.

explanations.concept: A thing at rest has balanced forces, not zero forces
explanations.definition: Forces on an object are balanced when they cancel each other exactly. The object then stays at rest if it was at rest.
explanations.description: The book has two forces on it: 5 newtons down from the Earth and 5 newtons up from the table. They are equal and opposite, so they cancel. Scientists say the forces are balanced. A balanced pair is not the same as no force. If you could switch off the table's push, the book would fall. If you could switch off gravity, nothing would hold the book to the table. Almost every still thing around you is held still by forces in balance. A building, a hanging lamp and a child sitting on a chair are all in the middle of a tie.
examples: In a tug of war where neither team moves, each team may be pulling with 2,000 newtons.
A picture on a wall: the nail pulls up, the Earth pulls down.
A pot on a tripod stand: three legs push up, and together their pushes equal the weight of the pot.
explanations.one_view: That balanced forces leave a resting object at rest is measured every time a scale is used. The older and wider views about motion come in the next card.
explanations.art: A tug of war with two teams leaning back hard, the rope straight and the centre flag exactly over the line.
explanations.context: This card shows that stillness is a balance of forces, with the numbers for a book on a table.

explanations.concept: A thing moving at a steady speed also has balanced forces
explanations.definition: If the forces on an object are balanced, its motion does not change. It stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed.
explanations.description: Most people believe that a moving thing needs a force to keep it moving. It feels true, because a cycle slows down when you stop pedalling. But the cycle slows because friction and air push backward on it. Suppose you pedal so that your forward push is exactly equal to those backward pushes. The forces are balanced. The cycle does not stop. It keeps going at a steady speed. So balanced forces do not mean 'not moving'. They mean 'not changing'. A force is needed to speed up, slow down or turn. No force is needed just to keep going.
examples: A carrom striker slides far on a powdered board, because the powder leaves very little friction to slow it.
The spacecraft Voyager 1 was launched in 1977. Its engines are off, and it is still moving away from the Sun at about 17 kilometres each second.
In a train moving steadily, a cup of tea on the table sits as still as it would at home.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, in Greece, about 350 BCE
perspectives.explanation: He taught that everything on Earth comes to rest unless something keeps pushing it. This fitted carts, ploughs and boats, and it was taught for nearly two thousand years.

perspectives.who: John Philoponus of Alexandria about 530 CE, and Ibn Sina in Persia about 1020 CE
perspectives.explanation: They argued that a thrower gives the thrown thing an inner push that carries it along. Ibn Sina added that in empty space this push would never fade. The Vaisheshika school in India described something similar and called it vega.

perspectives.who: Galileo Galilei in 1638 and Isaac Newton in 1687
perspectives.explanation: Galileo rolled balls on smoother and smoother slopes and saw them go further each time. He reasoned that with no friction a ball would never stop. Newton made this his first law of motion.

explanations.art: A cyclist on a flat road with a forward arrow at the back wheel and an equal backward arrow from the air and road, and a speedometer needle steady.
explanations.context: This card pushes against the belief that motion needs a force, and tells who first doubted it.

explanations.concept: The force diagram: draw one thing alone, with an arrow for each force on it
explanations.definition: A force diagram shows a single object with one arrow for each force acting on it. Each arrow points the way the force acts, and a longer arrow means a larger force.
explanations.description: When many things push on many things, it is easy to get lost. So scientists draw one thing only. Draw the thing as a dot or a box. Leave out the table, the hand and the rope. Then add an arrow for each force that acts on your thing, and label it with what is doing the pushing or pulling. Take a kite held steady in the sky. Three forces act on the kite. The Earth pulls it down. The string pulls it down and back towards the flier. The wind pushes it up and away from the flier. When the kite hangs still, the three arrows cancel.
examples: A book on a table: two arrows, weight down and support force up, of equal length.
A bucket being raised from a well at a steady speed: rope pulling up and weight down, of equal length.
A bucket just starting to rise: the rope's arrow is longer than the weight's arrow.
explanations.one_view: The force diagram is a drawing method that scientists and engineers share. It is a model, and like every model it leaves things out on purpose.
explanations.art: A kite in the sky on the left, and on the right the same kite drawn as a small diamond alone with four labelled arrows: weight, string, wind up and wind back.
explanations.context: This card teaches the drawing that lets you read the forces on any one thing.

explanations.concept: Friction points against sliding, and that is how it pushes you forward
explanations.definition: Friction is a force between two surfaces in contact. It acts along the surfaces, in the direction that stops them sliding past each other.
explanations.description: People say friction always slows things. Look at your foot as you walk. Your foot pushes backward on the ground. If the ground were ice, your foot would slide backward. Friction stops that slide. So the friction on your foot points forward. That forward friction is the force that moves you along. The same is true for a cycle and a bus. The tyre pushes backward on the road, and friction from the road pushes the tyre forward. Without friction no walker or wheel could start, turn or stop.
examples: On a wet bathroom floor there is little friction, so your foot slips backward and you do not go forward.
A bus stuck in mud spins its wheels. The wheels turn but the mud cannot give enough forward friction.
When you brake, friction from the road points backward on the tyre and slows you.
explanations.one_view: The direction of friction is settled and measured. What causes the grip is covered in the lessons on friction.
explanations.art: A side view of a walking foot with an arrow on the ground pointing backward labelled 'foot pushes ground' and an arrow on the shoe pointing forward labelled 'friction pushes foot'.
explanations.context: This card shows how to find the direction of friction, using walking as the example.

explanations.concept: Tension is the pull that runs along a tight rope, thread or chain
explanations.definition: Tension is the pulling force carried along a stretched rope, string, cable or chain. It pulls inward on whatever is tied at each end.
explanations.description: A rope cannot push. It can only pull, and only when it is tight. The pull that a tight rope carries is called tension. Tension acts along the rope. It pulls on the things at both ends, towards the middle of the rope. Hang a 2 kilogram bag of rice from a string. The Earth pulls the bag down with about 20 newtons. The string pulls up on the bag with 20 newtons. The same string pulls down on the hook with 20 newtons. A pulley, which is a wheel with a groove for a rope, can turn the direction of the tension. That is why you pull down on a well rope to bring the bucket up.
examples: A clothesline loaded with wet saris is under tension along its whole length.
The steel cables of a lift carry the weight of the cabin and the people in it.
A kite string is tight when the wind pulls the kite, and goes slack when the wind drops.
A spider hanging from her thread is held up by tension in the silk.
explanations.one_view: Tension is measured in every crane and bridge cable, and there is nothing in this description for scientists to dispute.
explanations.art: A well with a pulley, a rope going over it, a full bucket on one side and a pair of hands pulling down on the other, with arrows along the rope.
explanations.context: This card names the force in ropes and strings, which appears in many everyday force diagrams.

explanations.concept: Air and water push back on anything moving through them
explanations.definition: Air resistance and water resistance are forces that act on an object moving through air or water. They point against the motion and grow larger as the object moves faster.
explanations.description: Air is made of tiny particles. A thing moving through air must shove them aside, and they push back. This push is called air resistance. It has two features that friction between solids does not have. It grows as the speed grows: go twice as fast, and the push becomes about four times as large. It also depends on shape and size. A wide, flat thing meets more air than a narrow, pointed one. Now think of something falling. At first it speeds up. As it speeds up, the air pushes back harder. At some speed the push of the air equals the pull of gravity. The forces are balanced, and the thing falls at a steady speed from then on. This steady speed is called its terminal speed.
examples: A large raindrop falls at about 9 metres each second and no faster, however high the cloud.
A skydiver lying flat falls at about 200 kilometres per hour. When the parachute opens, its wide cloth meets far more air, and the steady speed drops to about 20.

In 2023 the Indian badminton player Satwiksairaj Rankireddy hit a smash measured at 565 kilometres per hour. The feathers of a shuttlecock catch so much air that the shuttle slows to a small part of that speed before it crosses the court.
Wading through a swimming pool is far harder than walking beside it, because water pushes back much more than air.
explanations.one_view: These speeds are measured, and the way air resistance grows with speed is used in designing every car and aeroplane.
explanations.art: Three drawings of one falling paper cone: at the start with a long weight arrow and a short air arrow, later with the air arrow longer, and last with the two arrows equal.
explanations.context: This card explains the force you test in the falling cones investigation.

explanations.concept: Upthrust: water and air push upward on things in them
explanations.definition: Upthrust is the upward push that a liquid or a gas gives to any object placed in it. It equals the weight of the liquid or gas that the object pushes aside.
explanations.description: Lower a steel tumbler into a bucket of water, open end up. You feel the water pushing up on it. That push is called upthrust. Water presses on a thing from all sides, and it presses harder deeper down. So the push on the bottom of the tumbler is greater than the push on the top, and the result is a push upward. About 250 BCE, Archimedes of Syracuse found the rule. The upthrust equals the weight of the water that the object pushes out of the way. If the upthrust can equal the object's weight, the object floats. If it cannot, the object sinks, but still feels lighter under water.
examples: A steel katori floats when set down gently, because its hollow shape pushes aside a lot of water. The same katori sinks when filled.
A big ship of steel floats for the same reason as the katori.
A stone that is hard to lift on the river bank is easier to lift under water.
Air gives upthrust too. A balloon filled with the light gas helium rises because the air pushes it up more strongly than the Earth pulls it down.
explanations.one_view: Archimedes' rule has been tested for more than two thousand years, and ships are built by it.
explanations.art: A steel katori floating in a bucket with water-pressure arrows all round it, longer underneath, and a second katori full of water sitting on the bottom.
explanations.context: This card adds the upward push of water and air, the force that holds up boats and fish.

explanations.concept: Magnetic force in a home: it acts across a gap and fades quickly with distance
explanations.definition: Magnetic force is the pull or push between magnets, and the pull of a magnet on iron, nickel and cobalt. It acts without touching.
explanations.description: A magnet pulls on a steel pin before they touch. The force crosses air, paper, cloth and your finger. It is strong close up and fades very quickly with distance. Pull a fridge magnet one centimetre away from the door and you can hardly feel the pull. A magnet pulls strongly on only a few materials: iron and steel, nickel and cobalt. It does not pull copper, aluminium, gold or wood. Every magnet has two ends called poles, north and south. Two like poles push each other apart, which scientists call repelling. Two unlike poles pull together, which is called attracting. The Earth is itself a huge, weak magnet, and that is why a compass needle turns to point north.
examples: A soft magnetic strip runs inside the rubber edge of a fridge door and holds the door shut.
The speaker in a phone and the motor in a toy car both have magnets inside.
Some pencil boxes, bag flaps and cupboard doors close with small magnets.
At a scrapyard, a crane with a magnet that can be switched on and off lifts steel and leaves plastic behind.

perspectives.who: Shen Kuo, in China, in his 'Dream Pool Essays' of about 1088 CE
perspectives.explanation: He described how to make a needle magnetic by rubbing it on a lodestone, a natural magnetic rock. He then hung the needle from a thread to find direction. He also noted that the needle points a little away from true south.

perspectives.who: William Gilbert, in England, in his book 'De Magnete' of 1600
perspectives.explanation: He shaped a lodestone into a ball and showed that small compass needles behave near it as real compasses behave on the Earth. He concluded that the Earth is a great magnet.

perspectives.who: Thales of Miletus, about 600 BCE, as reported by Aristotle in 'On the Soul'
perspectives.explanation: Thales is said to have held that the lodestone has a soul, because it moves iron. For him, whatever could cause movement by itself was alive in some way.

explanations.art: A fridge door cut away to show the magnetic strip in its rubber edge, with a compass on a nearby shelf whose needle points north.
explanations.context: This card places magnetic force in the home and tells how people came to know the Earth is a magnet.

explanations.concept: The static electric force: a rubbed comb pulls paper without touching
explanations.definition: The static electric force is the pull or push between objects that carry electric charge. Like the magnetic force, it acts across a gap.
explanations.description: Run a plastic comb through dry hair a few times and hold it near tiny pieces of paper. The pieces jump up to the comb. No magnet is involved, and paper is not iron. This is a different force, called the electric force. Rubbing moves some very small particles, called electrons, from the hair onto the comb. The comb now has extra electric charge. A charged thing pulls on light things nearby. Two things with the same kind of charge push each other apart. That is why freshly combed hair stands up and spreads: each hair is pushing the others away.
examples: A polyester shirt pulled off on a dry winter day crackles and clings.
A balloon rubbed on a woollen sweater sticks to a wall.
Dust gathers on a television screen because the screen becomes charged.
The Greek word for amber, a yellow tree gum, hardened over millions of years, that pulls dust when rubbed, is 'elektron'. The word electricity comes from it.
explanations.one_view: The electric force between charged objects was measured by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785 and is agreed. This test works best on a dry day and poorly in monsoon damp.
explanations.art: A plastic comb held just above scraps of paper, with several scraps in mid-air jumping up towards its teeth.
explanations.context: This card adds the second everyday force that acts without touching.

explanations.concept: How a muscle makes a pull
explanations.definition: Muscle force is the pull made when a muscle shortens. Inside the muscle, two kinds of protein thread slide past each other.
explanations.description: Every push you give begins as a pull by a muscle. A muscle is a bundle of long cells called fibres. Inside each fibre lie two kinds of very thin thread, made of proteins. One kind carries tiny heads along its length. When the muscle gets a signal from a nerve, each head grabs the other thread and tugs. Then it lets go and grabs again further along, like hands hauling a rope. The threads slide past each other and the fibre shortens. One head pulls with a force far too small to feel. A single muscle has many billions of heads, and their tiny pulls add up. This work uses energy from your food. Energy is what lets a body move things or change them.
examples: Your jaw muscles let your back teeth press together with a force of several hundred newtons, enough to crack a groundnut shell.
Your heart is a muscle that squeezes roughly 100,000 times a day without a rest.
An ant can carry 10 to 50 times their own weight.

perspectives.who: Jean Hanson with Hugh Huxley, and Andrew Huxley with Rolf Niedergerke, in two papers printed together in 1954
perspectives.explanation: Before 1954 most scientists thought the threads themselves shrank or folded. These four showed, with new microscopes, that the threads keep their length and slide past each other. Jean Hanson's share in this is often left out.

perspectives.who: Ayurvedic texts such as the Charaka Samhita
perspectives.explanation: They explain all movement in the body, from a blink to a step, by vata, the moving principle, linked with air and breath. This is an older account, framed differently from the measured one, and the two are not the same kind of claim.

explanations.art: A zoom-in from an arm to a muscle, to one fibre, to two kinds of thread with tiny heads on one thread gripping the other.
explanations.context: This card looks inside the body to show where muscle force comes from, and who found out.

explanations.concept: Your bones are levers, so a muscle often pulls much harder than the load weighs
explanations.definition: A lever is a stiff bar that turns about a fixed point. In the arm, the forearm bones are the bar, the elbow is the turning point and the muscle pulls close to the elbow.
explanations.description: Hold a one-litre bottle of water in your hand, with your elbow bent and your forearm level. The bottle weighs about 10 newtons. How hard is the muscle in your upper arm pulling? You might guess 10 newtons. The true answer is about 80. The muscle, called the biceps, is joined to the forearm only about 4 centimetres from the elbow. The bottle is about 32 centimetres from the elbow, which is 8 times as far. A pull close to the turning point must be much larger to balance a load far from it. So the muscle pulls with about 8 times the load. This is a simple picture, because other muscles share the work. What the body gains in return is speed and reach. A small shortening of the muscle swings the hand a long way.
examples: A door is hard to push near the hinges and easy to push at the handle. It is the same rule.
When you stand on tiptoe, your foot is a lever. The ball of the foot is the pivot, and the calf muscle pulls up on the heel bone.

A grasshopper's leg muscle pulls on a short lever inside the leg, and the long leg swings fast. The leg also stores the muscle's work in a springy part first, then lets go all at once, which throws the grasshopper many body lengths.
explanations.one_view: The lever rule goes back to Archimedes and has been checked on arms with instruments. The exact numbers differ from one person's arm to another's.
explanations.art: A bent arm drawn as a simple lever: the elbow as a pivot, the biceps attached 4 centimetres along with a long up arrow, and a bottle in the hand 32 centimetres along with a short down arrow.
explanations.context: This card gives the surprising numbers for muscle force in your own arm.

explanations.concept: Every living being meets the same forces, each in their own way
explanations.definition: Plants, animals and microbes sense and use gravity, grip, upthrust and magnetic force, each with their own body.
explanations.description: Forces are not only a matter for people and machines. A seed planted upside down still sends their root downward. Cells in the root tip hold tiny heavy grains. The grains settle to the lower side, so the root senses which way gravity points and grows that way. A gecko walks across a ceiling. Each toe carries a huge number of very fine hairs. The hairs come so close to the surface that a weak electric pull between hair and ceiling holds the gecko up. Most fish hold a small bag of gas inside the body and change its size to rise or sink. Some birds sense the Earth's magnetic field and steer by it on long journeys.
examples: Charles Darwin and his son Francis showed in 1880 that the tip of a root is the part that senses gravity.
Kellar Autumn and his colleagues measured the grip of a single gecko hair in 2000.
In the 1960s Wolfgang Wiltschko put European robins in a closed room. When he turned the magnetic field round them with coils, the robins changed the way they faced.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists such as Monica Gagliano and Stefano Mancuso
perspectives.explanation: A root tip takes in signals about gravity, water, touch and chemicals and settles on a direction. They describe this as deciding.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists such as Lincoln Taiz
perspectives.explanation: He and others reply that the settling grains and the growth chemicals they set moving fully explain the root's turn. They say a word like 'decide' fits animals with brains, and that a root needs no deciding.

explanations.art: Four small panels: a bean root curving downward from a sideways seed, a gecko upside down on a ceiling, a fish with a small gas bag shown inside, and a robin beside a compass.
explanations.context: This card shows how other beings sense and use the forces in this lesson.

explanations.concept: Underneath, only four kinds of force are known, and most everyday forces are one of them
explanations.definition: Physicists know of four basic forces: gravity, the electromagnetic force and two forces that act only inside the centres of atoms. Every everyday force except gravity is electromagnetic.
explanations.description: This lesson has named many forces. Underneath, physicists have found only four kinds. Two of them act only inside the tiny centre of an atom, and you never meet them directly. That leaves two for daily life. One is gravity. The other is the electromagnetic force, which is the electric force and the magnetic force together. The push of a table is this one force. So are the grip of friction, the pull in a rope, the push of air and the tug of a muscle. They come from electrons in the atoms of one thing pushing or pulling on the atoms of another. Even touch is this force. When you press a table, the electrons in your finger repel the electrons in the wood before the atoms ever meet.
examples: A small magnet lifts a steel pin off the floor. In that contest, one small magnet beats the gravity of the whole Earth, which shows how weak gravity is by comparison.
A rope holds because the atoms along each fibre attract their neighbours electrically.
Hans Christian Ørsted found in 1820 that an electric current turns a compass needle. In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell showed that electricity and magnetism are two sides of one force.

perspectives.who: Physicists since the 1970s, including Abdus Salam of Pakistan, Sheldon Glashow and Steven Weinberg
perspectives.explanation: They showed that the electromagnetic force and one of the forces inside the atom are two forms of one force. Many physicists hope that all four will turn out to be one.

perspectives.who: Physicists who think gravity is not a basic force like the others, such as Erik Verlinde
perspectives.explanation: They point out that gravity has refused to join the others for a hundred years. They think gravity may be a different kind of thing, which is the subject of the next card.

explanations.art: A zoom-in on a fingertip pressing a table: at the largest zoom, fuzzy clouds of electrons from the finger and from the wood facing each other across a small gap.
explanations.context: This card shows that the long list of everyday forces is really two forces, and that you never quite touch anything.

explanations.concept: What is gravity? We know how it acts, and nobody knows what it finally is
explanations.definition: Gravity is described very exactly by rules that predict how things fall and move. There is no agreed account of why masses draw towards each other.
explanations.description: You can predict to a fraction of a second when a dropped ball will land. That does not mean anyone knows what gravity is. Isaac Newton gave the rule for how strongly two masses pull each other. He was asked what causes the pull, and wrote that he would make no guess. In 1915 Albert Einstein gave a different picture. A mass such as the Earth bends the space and time around it, and things move along the bends. Here 'time' means what a clock measures. Clocks measure it very exactly, yet science cannot yet say what time finally is. In his picture a falling ball has no force on it at all. Both pictures predict everyday falling equally well. A third account, which would join gravity with the physics of tiny particles, does not yet exist.
examples: Satellite navigation on a phone works only because its sums include Einstein's bending of time near the Earth.

In 2015 instruments in the United States picked up ripples in space. They came from two black holes that crashed together far away, as Einstein's picture predicts. Another such instrument is being built at Hingoli in Maharashtra.

perspectives.who: Kanada, in the Vaisheshika Sutra 5.1.7, composed in India more than 2,000 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He states that when nothing holds a thing up, it falls because of gurutva, heaviness. He treats heaviness as a quality in the object that causes falling.

perspectives.who: Brahmagupta, in the Brahmasphutasiddhanta of 628 CE, and Bhaskara II, in the Siddhanta Shiromani of 1150 CE
perspectives.explanation: Brahmagupta wrote that things fall towards the Earth because it is the Earth's nature to draw them, as it is water's nature to flow. Bhaskara wrote that the Earth draws heavy things towards itself by its own power.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, in the second edition of his 'Principia', 1713
perspectives.explanation: Gravity is a pull between any two masses, across empty space. He gave its exact rule and wrote that he framed no hypotheses about its cause.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein, in 1915
perspectives.explanation: Gravity is not a pull. Mass bends space and time, and a falling thing is simply moving freely through bent space and time.

perspectives.who: Physicists who try to join gravity with the physics of tiny particles, such as Abhay Ashtekar
perspectives.explanation: Ashtekar works on the idea that space itself is made of tiny separate pieces. Others expect that gravity is carried by a particle called the graviton. No experiment has yet shown either.

explanations.art: A stretched cloth with a heavy ball in the middle making a dip and a marble circling the dip, beside a plain drawing of two balls joined by a pulling arrow, with a question mark between the two drawings.
explanations.context: This card says plainly where science runs out on gravity, with Indian and European views side by side.

explanations.concept: What is a force, really? A useful idea that may not be basic
explanations.definition: 'A force is a push or a pull' is a working definition. Physicists do not agree on whether force is a basic part of nature or a handy way of describing something deeper.
explanations.description: We have used the word force on every card. We can measure a force in newtons and predict what it will do. Can we say what a force is? Nobody has ever seen a force. We see a spring stretch or a ball speed up, and we say a force did it. Newton's own rule says that a force is what changes motion, which defines force by what it does. In modern physics the deepest descriptions do not use force at all. They use energy and things called fields, which fill space. Some physicists say force is only a useful everyday word, like 'sunrise'. So this is a word that sounds settled and is not. What do you think a force is?
examples: We say 'the Sun rises', and the phrase is useful, though it is the Earth that turns.
A force diagram of a kite predicts correctly whether the kite will climb, without telling us what an arrow is made of.

perspectives.who: Engineers and most physics teachers
perspectives.explanation: Force is as real as anything in science. Bridges stand and rockets fly because the forces were worked out correctly.

perspectives.who: Heinrich Hertz in 1894 and Ernst Mach in 1883
perspectives.explanation: Both tried to write the science of motion without force as a basic idea. They thought force was a name we give to a pattern in how things move, not a thing in itself.

perspectives.who: Frank Wilczek, a Nobel Prize physicist, writing in 2004
perspectives.explanation: He asked why the idea of force survives, when the deepest theories do without it. His answer was that force is a wonderfully practical way of thinking, and that this is not the same as being basic.

explanations.art: A spring balance stretched by a hanging mango, with a faint, dotted arrow beside it and a small question mark on the arrow.
explanations.context: This card admits that the main word of the lesson has no final definition, and invites the child's own thinking.

explanations.concept: Engineers arrange forces so that they balance: dams, bridges and nets
explanations.definition: A structure stands when every push and pull on each of its parts is balanced by another.
explanations.description: A bridge does not stand because it is strong in some general way. It stands because an engineer has traced where every force goes. The weight of a bus presses down on the deck. The deck pulls on cables or pushes on steel beams. The beams push on the towers, and the towers push on the ground. The ground pushes back. If one link cannot give the push or pull that is asked of it, the bridge falls. A dam must do the same against the sideways push of deep water. Good engineering is reading forces carefully before anything is built.
examples: The Kallanai dam on the Kaveri in Tamil Nadu was built of rough stone under the Chola king Karikala, about the 2nd century CE. It still turns the river's water into the fields today.

The Howrah Bridge in Kolkata, opened in 1943, hangs its road from two great steel arms that balance on two piers. Its steel is joined with rivets, which are metal pins hammered tight, and it has no nuts and bolts.
The Bandra-Worli Sea Link in Mumbai, opened in 2009, holds up its road with slanting steel cables in tension.
The big fishing nets at Fort Kochi in Kerala are balanced by stones hung on ropes at the back. A few people can raise a net wider than a room.
explanations.one_view: This is how structures are designed everywhere. The builders of Kallanai knew it by experience long before force diagrams existed.
explanations.art: A cable-stayed bridge with arrows showing the bus's weight going down, along the cables as tension, down the tower and into the ground, where an arrow pushes back up.
explanations.context: This card shows how reading forces is used to build things that stand for centuries.

agreed.text: With no air, a hammer and a feather fall side by side.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 the astronaut David Scott stood on the Moon, which has no air, and dropped a hammer and a falcon's feather from the same height. Both reached the dust at the same moment. The film can be watched today.

agreed.text: The pull of gravity is very slightly different from place to place on the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Instruments on satellites and on the ground measure it. The pull is a little weaker at the equator than at the poles, and a little weaker on a mountain than at the sea. A band of slightly weaker pull also lies under the Indian Ocean, south of Sri Lanka, for reasons scientists are still working out.

agreed.text: The Earth's magnetic north pole is not fixed. It wanders, and the whole magnetic field has flipped over many times in the past.
agreed.evidence: Since the pole was first located in 1831, it has moved more than 2,000 kilometres across the Arctic. Lava records the direction of the field as it cools. Layers of old lava, including the Deccan Traps of Maharashtra, show the field pointing one way and then the other.

agreed.text: Muscles and bones weaken when the usual forces are taken away.
agreed.evidence: Astronauts who live for months in a space station lose bone and muscle, even with two hours of exercise a day. The main reason is that their bodies are not pressed against a floor. Doctors measure the loss when they return.

challenging.claim: Gravity is not a basic force at all. It arises from something deeper, the way the push of air on a wall comes from many moving particles hitting it.
challenging.who: Erik Verlinde, a Dutch physicist, in 2010, building on work by Ted Jacobson in 1995
challenging.for: The mathematics of gravity looks surprisingly like the mathematics of heat. Verlinde showed that Newton's rule for gravity can be worked out from ideas about information and heat alone.
challenging.against: Most physicists are not persuaded. Tests of his idea against the motions of galaxies have given mixed results, and nobody has shown what the 'something deeper' is made of.
challenging.context: This view challenges the list of four basic forces. It is here to show that even gravity's place on the list is questioned.

challenging.claim: Newton's rule for gravity needs changing where the pull is extremely weak.
challenging.who: Mordehai Milgrom, an Israeli physicist, in 1983
challenging.for: Stars at the edges of galaxies go round faster than Newton's rule allows for the matter we can see. Milgrom's small change to the rule predicts those speeds well for many galaxies.
challenging.against: Most astronomers explain the fast stars by unseen 'dark matter' instead. Milgrom's change does not work well for great clusters of galaxies. Nobody has yet caught a particle of dark matter either.
challenging.context: Two camps of scientists disagree about whether the law of gravity or our list of matter is incomplete.

challenging.claim: A moving thing needs a force to keep it moving.
challenging.who: Aristotle, about 350 BCE, and nearly everyone's common sense today
challenging.for: Every cart, cycle and ball we push does stop when we stop pushing. Studies show that most adults, even after school physics, still think this way.
challenging.against: The stopping is caused by friction and air resistance, which are forces. Where these are very small, as for a spacecraft, things keep moving for decades with no push.
challenging.context: This is the most common belief about force and motion. It is wrong, and it is worth seeing why it feels right.

challenging.claim: Plants do not merely respond to gravity. They sense, weigh up and decide.
challenging.who: Monica Gagliano, Stefano Mancuso and other researchers in plant behaviour, since about 2005
challenging.for: A root tip responds to gravity, water, touch, light and chemicals together, and what the root does cannot be predicted from any one of them. Plants also behave differently after experience.
challenging.against: In 2019 Lincoln Taiz and seven other plant scientists wrote a reply. They said plants lack the body parts that go with experience and choice in animals. They said chemistry alone can explain the results.
challenging.context: Scientists agree on what roots do. They disagree about which words describe it truly.

big_questions.q: A book on a table has two large forces on it and does nothing. Is anything happening to the book?
big_questions.hint: Imagine one of the two forces vanishing. Then ask if 'doing nothing' is the right description of what was there before.

big_questions.q: Your finger never truly touches the table, because electrons push apart first. So what do you mean when you say you touched something?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you feel in your fingertip and where that feeling is made.

big_questions.q: Nobody has ever seen a force, only what forces do. Is a force a real thing, or an idea we use to explain what we see?
big_questions.hint: Think of other things you know only by what they do, such as the wind. Is the wind real?

big_questions.q: Einstein said a falling ball has no force on it. Newton said gravity pulls it. Both predict the same landing. Can both be right?
big_questions.hint: Ask what job each picture is doing. Then ask what would have to be found to choose between them.

big_questions.q: A fish held up by water does not feel their own weight. Is there something holding you up all the time that you have stopped noticing?
big_questions.hint: Start with the floor. Then think more widely about what you lean on every day.

big_questions.q: You pull the Earth exactly as hard as the Earth pulls you. Why does it feel as if only the Earth is doing the pulling?
big_questions.hint: Think about who moves more when a small child and a large adult push off from each other on roller skates.

big_questions.q: A root senses which way is down and grows that way. Is the root deciding, or only being moved?
big_questions.hint: Ask what you would need to see before you said that a friend had decided something. Then check the root against your own list.

big_questions.q: A bridge stands because every force is passed on to something else, down to the ground. What is the ground passing its forces on to?
big_questions.hint: Follow the push downward as far as you can. Does the chain have an end?

big_questions.q: When two people disagree and neither gives way, nothing moves. Is that like balanced forces, and is it the same as peace?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tug of war rope that is still. What is going on inside the rope?

story.title: The Net That Was Not Resting
story.note: A made-up story set at Fort Kochi in Kerala. The people are imagined. The big shore nets are real. Each is a wooden frame that tips like a see-saw on a post, with a net at the front and stones hung on ropes at the back, and is worked by a small crew. People in Kochi say that traders from China brought the design about 600 years ago, and historians are not sure. Most fish hold a small bag of gas in the body that lets the water carry their weight.
text: Joel, who was seven, thought the big fishing net at Fort Kochi was asleep. It stood over the water like a giant spider made of teak poles and rope, and not one part of it moved. His cousin Nilofer, who was ten, had brought him at dawn to watch Rosy chechi's crew. Rosy had worked this net for twenty years, and now she led its crew of five.
'It is not doing anything,' said Joel.
'Put your hand on this rope,' said Rosy chechi.
He did. The rope was as hard as an iron rod, and it hummed under his palm.

'That rope is pulling up on the net as hard as it can,' she said. 'The net is pulling down on the rope just as hard. Neither one wins. That is why you see nothing.' She pointed to the back of the frame, where a row of big stones hung in the air, each on a rope of its own. 'The Earth pulls those stones down. The stones pull the back of the frame down. The frame tips on that post like a see-saw. So the stones behind us are holding up the net in front of us.'

Nilofer liked to work things out one piece at a time. 'Take one stone,' she said. 'The Earth pulls it down. The rope pulls it up. The two are equal, so the stone hangs still.' She looked at her own feet. 'And me. The Earth pulls me down, and the planks push me up.' She jumped. The planks creaked. 'They push harder when I land.'

Old Kunjumon was mending a float nearby. He snorted. 'Forty years I have hauled this net. I never drew an arrow. The net is heavy when the tide runs and light when the water is slack. My shoulders know.'
'Your shoulders are measuring the same pulls she is counting,' said Rosy chechi.
'Arrows do not get tired,' said Kunjumon. 'So arrows miss half of it.'
Nobody had an answer to that.

Rosy chechi called out, and the crew walked forward along the main beam. Their weight tipped the see-saw. The net sank under the water, and the stones at the back rose. Everyone waited. Then the crew walked back and hauled on the ropes. The stones came down, one after another, and the net came up streaming. Joel hauled too. The rope pulled on his arms exactly as hard as he pulled on the rope.

In the net a dozen small silver fish were flapping. Nilofer watched one of them. 'In the water they were not heavy,' she said slowly. 'The water pushed up on them as hard as the Earth pulled down. They never had to hold themselves up. Now the water is gone, and only the net is holding them.'
'First time in their lives they meet their whole weight,' said Rosy chechi. She tipped the smallest ones back into the sea.
'So in the water they had no weight?' asked Joel.
'No,' said Nilofer. 'The Earth was pulling them the whole time. They could not feel it, because something was pushing back from every side.' She stopped. 'Like us. We do not feel the planks pushing.'
Kunjumon looked up from his float. 'Then what is it that I feel, when the net is heavy?'
Nilofer thought for a long time. 'You feel your own muscle pulling one way and the rope pulling the other. You feel what it is like to be in the middle.'
The old man grunted, and went back to his knot. But he was smiling a little.

The Sun was up now. The net hung over the water again, quite still. Joel looked at it, and this time he could see. The rope was tight. The stones hung. The post pressed into the mud, and the mud pressed back. The wind leaned on the poles. A crow sat on the highest pole, and the crow's toes gripped the wood.
'It is not asleep,' he said. 'It is a tug of war, and everybody is winning the same amount.'
'Nobody is winning,' said Rosy chechi. 'That is what standing still is.'
Joel looked along the shore, at the boats, the wall and the sea. 'Is there anything, anywhere, that nothing is pulling or pushing?'
Rosy chechi looked at the water for a while. 'I have never met one,' she said. 'If you find one, bring it to me.'
story.epiphany: The still net was held by pulls and pushes in exact balance. The fish were carried by the water without feeling it, as Joel was carried by the planks. Standing still turned out to be something that many things do together.
ask: Kunjumon said arrows miss half of it. What do his shoulders know that a force diagram leaves out?
The fish did not feel their weight until the water was gone. What holds you up that you have never noticed?
Joel asked if there is anything that nothing pulls or pushes. What would you look at first to find out?
Rosy chechi said nobody is winning, and that is what standing still is. Do you agree?
art: A tall wooden fishing frame at the water's edge at dawn, with a wide net hanging at the front and a row of stones hanging on ropes at the back.

The net lifted out of the sea, streaming water, with small silver fish in the bottom and a girl bending to look.

how_we_found_out.story: For nearly two thousand years, people who studied nature followed Aristotle. He taught that heavy things fall faster than light ones, in proportion to their weight, and that anything moving stops unless pushed. Both ideas fitted daily life: a stone beats a leaf to the ground, and a cart stops when the bullock does. About 530 CE, John Philoponus in Alexandria wrote that he had dropped two weights, one many times heavier than the other. He said they landed at almost the same moment. Few listened. In 1586 Simon Stevin in Holland dropped two lead balls, one ten times the weight of the other, from a church tower onto a wooden board. They struck with one sound. In 1638 Galileo Galilei, in Italy, published his own tests with balls rolling down slopes. He showed that falling things gain speed steadily, and reasoned that a leaf lags only because the air holds it back. In 1687 Isaac Newton gathered all this into three laws of motion and one rule for gravity. In 1971 an astronaut on the airless Moon dropped a hammer and a feather together, and the world watched them land as one.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, John Philoponus, Simon Stevin, Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton, David Scott
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People held that heavier things fall faster, and that motion needs a constant push. Both were believable because air resistance and friction are always present on Earth and hide what gravity alone does. Tests that made the hidden forces small showed the truth.

roots.context: You have learnt to read the forces on still and moving things. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves, about life and about this world.

deep_truth.truth: On the scale under the books, the number went up when you pressed down and went down when you lifted, though nothing moved. The scale does not read the pull of the Earth by itself. It reads how hard its own top pushes up. So the weight you feel on a scale, or on your feet, is a push from below, and that push changes by exactly the amount needed.
deep_truth.habit: We think weight is something a thing simply has, like its colour. But a scale and your feet feel the push of a surface. Take the surface away, as in a falling lift, and the feeling of weight goes, though the Earth pulls just as hard.
deep_truth.evidence: In the scale test, pressing on the books raised the reading and lifting them lowered it, while the books stayed put. In the cone test, the push of the air grew until it matched the weight. In both, a push grew until it matched what it met.

three.who_am_i: As you sit reading, what you feel as your weight is the chair pushing up on you. Your muscles pull on your bones, and your heart squeezes roughly 100,000 times a day. Feeling heavy is really feeling held up by the chair, the Earth and your own body together.
three.what_is_life: A root senses the pull of the Earth and grows down. A fish lets the water carry their weight. A muscle is billions of tiny pulls added together. Every living being lives by reading forces and answering them, and is never outside them.
three.what_is_this_world: Follow the push under a book and you go from the table to the floor, then to the ground and the whole Earth. The Sun holds the Earth in its path. No object has been found that nothing pushes or pulls. The world is joined all the way through by these pushes and pulls.

roots.thread: This lesson asked you to pick one thing and list the forces on it. Every list led to other things: the table, the rope, the water, the Earth. You could not finish describing one thing without bringing in the rest. That is a plain finding about forces. It suggests that a 'separate thing' is not as separate as it looks. Some teachers of oneness go one step further. They say consciousness is the ground from which every thing and every force arises. In their words, the balance holding a book on a table is that one ground holding itself. Many scientists accept the finding and not this last step, and their view is given below.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says that the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people.
teachings.link: The verse is about how a person should act, not about tables. The lesson's science gives a small, exact picture of its second half. A book lying still is the meeting point of two forces that never stop acting.

teachings.source: Heraclitus of Ephesus, about 500 BCE, fragment 51 in the Diels and Kranz numbering
teachings.teaching: He wrote that people do not understand how a thing can agree with itself while pulling apart. There is a harmony of opposite pulls, as in the bow and the lyre.
teachings.link: A bow keeps its shape because wood and string pull against each other. The fishing net, the bridge and the tug of war rope in this lesson stand in the same way.

teachings.teaching: Laozi writes that nothing in the world is softer or more yielding than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard and strong.
teachings.link: Water gives way to a finger and still holds up a ship. The lesson measured that upward push. Laozi draws from it a teaching about how to live, which science neither supports nor denies.

science.text: Every force is one side of a pair. When the Earth pulls you, you pull the Earth equally. No force has ever been found acting alone.
Ernst Mach proposed that a thing's resistance to being pushed comes from all the other matter in the universe. Einstein took the idea seriously. It has never been confirmed or ruled out.

other_view.who: Physicalist scientists, and the Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: Balanced forces are a matter of adding numbers. In this view nothing is 'holding' or 'keeping' anything, and a table does not act. Words like holding and keeping are only a way of speaking. The joined-up picture is true as physics, and it shows no ground beneath physics.

practice.title: Feeling the floor push back
practice.say: Stand with your feet a little apart and close your eyes. Feel the soles of your feet. The floor is pushing up on them, exactly as hard as the Earth is pulling you down. Now lean very slowly forward, then back, and feel the push move under your toes and your heels. Come back to the middle. Take three slow breaths, and notice that you are being held up without doing anything.
practice.kid: Stand still and close your eyes. Feel the floor pushing up on your feet. Lean slowly forward and back, and feel the push move. Stand in the middle and take three slow breaths. Notice that the floor is holding you.

ask: When you stand still, are you doing something or doing nothing?
You could not list the forces on a book without naming the table and the Earth. Can you describe yourself without naming anything else?
If no thing has ever been found that nothing pushes or pulls, what does 'alone' mean?
roots.art: A child standing barefoot with eyes closed, small up arrows under each foot and one down arrow from the chest, the arrows the same length.

open_questions.q: What is gravity, and can it be joined with the physics of tiny particles?
open_questions.why_open: Einstein's picture of bent space and time passes every test at large sizes. The physics of particles passes every test at tiny sizes. The two cannot both be complete, and no experiment has yet reached the place where they meet.

open_questions.q: Why is gravity so much weaker than the other forces?
open_questions.why_open: A small magnet beats the whole Earth's pull on a pin. Between two of the particles inside an atom, the electric force is stronger than gravity by a number with 36 zeros. No accepted theory explains so great a difference.

open_questions.q: Are the four basic forces really one?
open_questions.why_open: Two of the four were shown to be one in the 1970s. Theories that join a third have predicted effects that experiments have not found. Gravity has not been joined at all.

open_questions.q: How exactly do birds sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: One idea is tiny magnetic grains in the beak. Another is a light-sensitive molecule in the eye that responds to magnetism. Experiments support each in part, and the birds may use both.

open_questions.q: Is force a basic part of nature?
open_questions.why_open: The deepest theories of physics are written in terms of energy and fields and do not need force. Yet force describes everyday life very well. Physicists and philosophers still discuss which description is closer to what is there.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull on something. A force can start a thing moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, turn it or squash it.
terms.example: You pull a drawer open. Your hand's pull is a force on the drawer.
terms.art: A child pulling a steel drawer open with one hand, a small arrow showing the pull.

terms.meaning: A force that moves a thing away from whatever is pushing it.
terms.example: You push a swing away from you, and it goes forward.
terms.art: A child pushing a swing with both hands, an arrow pointing forward from the swing.

terms.meaning: A force that moves a thing towards whatever is pulling it.
terms.example: You pull a bucket up from a well, and it comes towards you.
terms.art: A child hauling a rope hand over hand, an arrow along the rope towards her.

terms.meaning: The pull that the Earth has on everything, and everything has on the Earth. It acts towards the middle of the Earth.
terms.example: A coconut that comes loose from a palm falls straight down because of gravity.
terms.art: A coconut dropping from a palm tree with a long arrow pointing down.

terms.meaning: The size of the pull of the Earth on a thing, measured in newtons. A heavier thing has a bigger weight.
terms.example: A one-kilogram bag of sugar has a weight of about 10 newtons.
terms.art: A bag of sugar on a hook with an arrow down labelled 10 newtons.

terms.meaning: The unit we use to measure a force. A small apple is pulled down by the Earth with about one newton.
terms.example: A child of 30 kilograms is pulled down with 300 newtons, near enough.
terms.art: A small apple in a hand beside the label 1 newton.

terms.meaning: How much stuff a thing is made of, measured in kilograms. A thing has the same mass on the Earth, on the Moon and in space.
terms.example: A packet of 2 kilograms of rice has a mass of 2 kilograms in your kitchen and the same mass on the Moon.
terms.art: A kitchen scale with a rice packet on it showing 2 kilograms.

terms.meaning: The middle point deep inside the planet. Gravity pulls everything towards it, so 'down' always means towards it.
terms.example: A child in Chennai and a child in Mexico are both pulled towards the centre, so their 'down' directions point nearly opposite ways.
terms.art: A cut-away round Earth with two small children standing on opposite sides, arrows pointing to the middle.

terms.meaning: Feeling no push from the floor or the seat, so that you float. A weightless person is still being pulled by gravity.
terms.example: At the very top of a jump on a trampoline, for a moment, you feel weightless.
terms.art: A child at the top of a trampoline jump with the springy mat far below and a small arrow pointing down.

terms.meaning: The curved path of something that keeps falling round a planet, a moon or a star, and keeps missing it.
terms.example: The International Space Station goes round the Earth in an orbit, about once every 90 minutes.
terms.art: A small station circling a blue Earth with a curved dotted path and an arrow pointing in to the Earth.

terms.meaning: The push that a surface gives upward on anything resting on it.
terms.example: The table pushes up on a book with the support force.
terms.art: A book on a table with an upward arrow from the table top to the book.

terms.meaning: The outside layer of a thing, the place where it touches other things.
terms.example: The top of a table is a surface, and so is the skin of your hand.
terms.art: A hand resting flat on a wooden table, the touching place marked in red.

terms.meaning: Forces on one thing that are equal and point in opposite ways, so they cancel each other out.
terms.example: A book on a table has 5 newtons down and 5 newtons up, so the forces on it are balanced.
terms.art: A book with two equal arrows, one up and one down, and an equals sign between them.

terms.meaning: Not moving at all compared with the ground or the room you are in.
terms.example: A school bag lying on a chair is at rest.
terms.art: A school bag lying on a chair in a quiet classroom.

terms.meaning: Moving at the same speed in the same direction, with no speeding up, slowing down or turning.
terms.example: A ceiling fan blade turning at the same rate for an hour has a steady speed.
terms.art: A cyclist on a long straight road with evenly spaced milestones beside her.

terms.meaning: The force between two surfaces that touch. It tries to stop them sliding past each other.
terms.example: A chappal grips the road because of friction, and slips on a wet floor because there is less of it.
terms.art: A chappal on a rough road with a small arrow along the ground pointing forward.

terms.meaning: The push of the air against anything moving through it. It points against the motion and grows as the speed grows.
terms.example: Hold your hand flat out of a bus window. The air pushes it backward.
terms.art: A hand held flat out of a moving bus window with arrows of air pushing against it.

terms.meaning: A drawing of one thing alone, with one arrow for every force that acts on it.
terms.example: A force diagram of a book on a table shows a dot or box with two arrows, one up and one down.
terms.art: A box on a page with two arrows, one up and one down, each with a label.

terms.meaning: In a force diagram, a line with a point at the end. The point shows the way the force acts, and a longer arrow shows a bigger force.
terms.example: A long arrow down and a short arrow up on a falling leaf shows that gravity is winning.
terms.art: Two arrows of different lengths pointing opposite ways from the same dot.

terms.meaning: The pull that runs along a tight rope, string, cable or chain.
terms.example: A bag hanging from a string is held up by the tension in the string.
terms.art: A bag of rice hanging from a thread with an arrow up along the thread.

terms.meaning: A wheel with a groove for a rope. It turns the direction of a pull.
terms.example: A well pulley lets you pull the rope down to bring the bucket up.
terms.art: A wheel hung over a well with a rope running over it and a bucket on one side.

terms.meaning: A very thick rope made of twisted steel wires. It carries tension.
terms.example: The slanting cables of the Bandra-Worli Sea Link in Mumbai hold up its road.
terms.art: A bridge tower with slanting cables fanning out to the road.

terms.meaning: The steady speed at which a falling thing stops speeding up, because the push of the air has grown as big as its weight.
terms.example: A large raindrop reaches a terminal speed of about 9 metres in each second.
terms.art: A raindrop falling from a cloud with a long arrow down and a growing arrow up that ends equal to it.

terms.meaning: A wide piece of cloth that catches a lot of air. The push of the air is then large, and the faller reaches a slow terminal speed.
terms.example: A skydiver falls at about 200 kilometres per hour, and with the parachute open at about 20.
terms.art: A skydiver under a wide round parachute, with a big arrow up and an equal arrow down.

terms.meaning: The upward push that water or air gives to anything put in it.
terms.example: When you push an empty bucket down in water, you feel the water pushing it back up. That push is upthrust.
terms.art: An empty plastic bucket pushed down in a bigger tub, with an arrow up from the water.

terms.meaning: To stay up on the top of a liquid, because the upthrust equals the weight.
terms.example: A steel katori set gently on water floats.
terms.art: A steel katori floating on water with two equal arrows, down and up.

terms.meaning: To go down in a liquid, because the weight is bigger than the biggest upthrust the water can give.
terms.example: A steel spoon sinks in water.
terms.art: A steel spoon at the bottom of a glass of water with a long arrow down and a short arrow up.

terms.meaning: A piece of iron, steel or other metal that pulls on iron and on other magnets without touching them.
terms.example: A fridge magnet holds a paper on the fridge door.
terms.art: A horseshoe magnet and a steel pin that is leaping up towards it.

terms.meaning: The pull or push of a magnet, which acts across a gap.
terms.example: A magnet pulls a steel paper clip across a table before it touches it.
terms.art: A magnet above a steel clip with a dotted gap between them and a small arrow.

terms.meaning: One of the two ends of a magnet, where the force is strongest. They are called north and south.
terms.example: A bar magnet has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
terms.art: A bar magnet with the ends labelled N and S.

terms.meaning: To pull together. Unlike poles of two magnets attract.
terms.example: A north pole and a south pole snap together.
terms.art: Two bar magnets end to end, pulling each other, with arrows pointing inwards.

terms.meaning: To push apart. Like poles of two magnets repel.
terms.example: Two north poles pushed together slide away from each other on a table.
terms.art: Two bar magnets with the same poles facing, with arrows pointing outwards.

terms.meaning: A rock that is a natural magnet. It was found in the ground long before people made magnets.
terms.example: The Greek thinker Thales, about 600 BCE, is reported to have thought that a lodestone has a soul, because it moves iron.
terms.art: A dark knobbly rock with iron filings stuck to one end.

terms.meaning: A small instrument with a magnetic needle that is free to turn. The needle points to the north.
terms.example: A walker in a forest turns the compass until the needle matches N, and then knows which way is north.
terms.art: A round compass lying on a hand, the needle pointing at N.

terms.meaning: A property of tiny particles that makes them push or pull each other. There are two kinds, called positive and negative.
terms.example: A rubbed comb gets electric charge and pulls tiny paper bits.
terms.art: A plastic comb above small paper bits, with plus and minus signs on the comb.

terms.meaning: A very small particle, found in every atom, that carries negative electric charge.
terms.example: Rubbing a balloon on wool moves electrons from the wool to the balloon.
terms.art: A tiny dot with a minus sign circling a bigger round atom.

terms.meaning: The pull or push between things that have electric charge, when the charge stays where it is.
terms.example: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall because of the static electric force.
terms.art: A balloon on a wall with small plus and minus signs along the contact.

terms.meaning: A part of the body made of fibres that can shorten and so pull on a bone.
terms.example: The muscle in your upper arm pulls your forearm up.
terms.art: An arm with the upper arm muscle drawn as a bulge and a pull arrow to the forearm.

terms.meaning: A long thin thread. A muscle fibre is a long cell that shortens when it works.
terms.example: A strip of cooked chicken pulls apart into long fibres.
terms.art: A muscle opened out to show bundles of long thin fibres.

terms.meaning: A big molecule made by living cells. Proteins do much of the work in a body, such as making muscles pull.
terms.example: Dal, eggs, curd and paneer contain protein.
terms.art: A bowl of dal beside a drawing of a tangled molecule.

terms.meaning: What lets anything move, heat up or change. Food gives a body energy, and fuel gives a bus energy. We can measure it, but science cannot yet say what energy finally is.
terms.example: A child who has eaten a banana has the energy to run across the playground.
terms.art: A child eating a banana on the left and running on the right, joined by a curved arrow.

terms.meaning: A long bundle of fibres that carries signals between the body and the brain.
terms.example: A nerve carries the signal 'pull' to the muscle in your arm.
terms.art: A line from a brain down the spine to an arm muscle, with small signal dots.

terms.meaning: A stiff bar that turns about one fixed point. A small push far from that point can balance a big push near it.
terms.example: A see-saw is a lever with its middle as the turning point.
terms.art: A see-saw with a small child far out and a big child near the middle, level.

terms.meaning: The fixed point that a lever turns about.
terms.example: The elbow is the pivot of the forearm. The hinge is the pivot of a door.
terms.art: A door seen from above with its hinge marked as a dot.

terms.meaning: The muscle at the front of your upper arm. It pulls the forearm up when it shortens.
terms.example: Bend your arm with a bag in your hand and feel the biceps tighten.
terms.art: An arm bent upward with the biceps bulging and a pull arrow to the forearm.

terms.meaning: A tiny piece of matter, much too small to see. Everything we touch is made of atoms.
terms.example: A single grain of salt holds roughly a million million million atoms.
terms.art: A single round atom with a small nucleus and tiny dots around it.

terms.meaning: The one force that includes both the electric force and the magnetic force. It holds atoms together and is behind pushes by tables, ropes and muscles.
terms.example: A table pushes up on a book through the electromagnetic force between their atoms.
terms.art: Two groups of atoms in a table and a book, with small arrows pushing between them.

terms.meaning: A region of space where a force can be felt by something placed there.
terms.example: A magnet has a magnetic field around it. A paper clip that enters the field feels a pull.
terms.art: A bar magnet with curved lines looping from one end to the other.

terms.meaning: What a clock measures: the seconds, minutes and hours between one thing happening and another. Clocks measure it very exactly, but science cannot yet say what time finally is.
terms.example: A cone that falls for 1.5 seconds has taken 1.5 seconds of time, as the stopwatch shows.
terms.art: A phone stopwatch showing 1.5 seconds beside a paper cone in mid-fall.

terms.meaning: Something built from parts that hold each other up, such as a bridge, a dam or a building.
terms.example: A bridge is a structure. The deck, cables, towers and ground all pass forces to each other.
terms.art: A small bridge with arrows following the force from the road to the ground.

terms.meaning: A metal pin that is hammered through two steel plates and flattened at both ends to join them.
terms.example: The Howrah Bridge in Kolkata is joined with rivets and has no nuts and bolts.
terms.art: Two steel plates joined by a pin with flattened ends.

terms.meaning: A wall built across a river to hold water back. It must resist the sideways push of deep water.
terms.example: The Kallanai dam on the Kaveri in Tamil Nadu has held back water for about two thousand years.
terms.art: A stone dam across a river with an arrow of water pushing sideways on it.

items.f: A book lying on a table.
items.b: Weight, down. Support force, up. Equal and opposite, so the forces on the book are balanced.

items.f: A school bag hanging on a hook by its strap.
items.b: Weight, down. Tension in the strap, up. They are equal.

items.f: A fish hanging still in the water, not rising or sinking.
items.b: Weight, down. Upthrust, up. They are equal.

items.f: A steel pin held in the air under a magnet by a thread tied to the table, not touching the magnet.
items.b: Weight, down. Tension in the thread, down. Magnetic force, up. The up pull equals the two down pulls.

items.f: A big raindrop falling at its steady speed.
items.b: Weight, down. Air resistance, up. They are equal, so the raindrop stops speeding up.

items.f: A skydiver falling under an open parachute at a steady speed.
items.b: Weight, down. Air resistance, up. They are equal at a slow steady speed.

items.f: A bucket being pulled up a well at a steady speed.
items.b: Weight, down. Tension in the rope, up. They are equal, because the speed is steady.

items.f: A cyclist pedalling at a steady speed on a flat road.
items.b: Weight, down. Support force from the road, up. Friction from the road, forward. Air resistance, backward. Down balances up, and forward balances backward.

items.f: A child standing still on the floor.
items.b: Weight, down. Support force from the floor, up. They are equal.

items.f: A rubbed balloon stuck to a wall and not sliding down.
items.b: Weight, down. Friction, up. Electric force, towards the wall. Support force, away from the wall. Each pair is equal.

items.f: A boat floating still on a lake.
items.b: Weight, down. Upthrust, up. They are equal.

items.f: A ceiling fan hanging from its rod and not turning.
items.b: Weight, down. Tension in the rod, up. They are equal.

items.f: A kite held steady in the sky by a string.
items.b: Weight, down. Tension in the string, down and towards the flier. Wind pushing on the kite, up and away from the flier. All three cancel.

items.f: A forearm holding a bottle still, with the elbow bent at a right angle.
items.b: Weight of the bottle and the arm, down. Muscle pull of the biceps, up. Support force from the elbow, down. Up balances down.

items.f: A carrom coin sliding along a powdered board and slowing down.
items.b: Weight, down. Support force, up. Friction, backward. Friction is not balanced, so the coin slows.

items.f: A cricket ball at the very top of a throw, for one instant not moving.
items.b: Weight, down. Air resistance is almost nothing at that moment. The ball is not moving, but its weight is not balanced, so it starts falling.

items.f: DEBATE CARD. A spacecraft going round the Earth with its engines off. Is there a force on it?
items.b: Two answers can both be defended. Newton: gravity pulls it all the time, and that pull bends its path. Einstein: there is no force on it, and it follows the bend that the Earth makes in space and time. Score 2 points for either answer if you give one reason.

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: a row for each round 1 to 8 and a column for each player
items: Round 1 to round 8: points for each player.
Total points for each player.

rules: There are 9 kinds of force card, four of each, and 17 thing cards. The thing cards have the answer on the back.
Deal 6 force cards to each player. The rest are the draw pile. If the draw pile runs out, shuffle the used cards and use them again.
A round begins when one player reads the front of the top thing card aloud and puts it in the middle, answer down.
Before betting, each player may swap up to 2 force cards for new ones from the draw pile.
Each player secretly puts down between 1 and 4 force cards, face down, for the forces they think are acting on that thing. Then all turn their cards over together.

Turn the thing card over and read the answer. Each force card you played that is on the answer scores 2 points. Each force card you played that is not on the answer loses 1 point. If you play two cards of the same kind, only one can score and the other loses a point. Your total for a round is never below 0.
