Bonus: for each correct card you also say the direction of the force aloud before the card is turned. A correct direction scores 1 more point.

On the debate card, either answer scores 2 points. Play the weight card to say that gravity is a force on it. Or play no card at all to say that there is no force. You must give one reason, and the other players decide if it is a real reason.
After each round, used cards go in a discard pile. Each player draws back up to 6 cards.
Play 8 rounds. The player with the most points wins. A tie is shared. A tie can be settled by playing one more thing card.
Many things have more than one force on them. The back of the card lists every force that matters.

flow.do: Cut out the 36 force cards and the 17 thing cards from the printed sheet. Shuffle the force cards and the thing cards separately. Put the answers on the thing cards face down, so that nobody sees them.
flow.say: These cards are forces. Each thing card shows something from everyday life. Which forces do you think are acting on it?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle the two piles.
flow.parent: A grown-up can cut the cards for a child under 8. Keep them in an envelope for the next game.

flow.do: Play one practice round with the thing card about a book on a table. Show how to bet. Talk about each force card that is played and why.
flow.say: Which force cards would you play for a book on a table? Why those?
flow.kid: Practice with one thing card. Put down your force cards.
flow.parent: In the practice round, give each child time to say why. A wrong bet loses a point, but the point of the game is to find out why, not to win.

flow.do: Play 8 rounds with the rules. After each round, read the back of the card aloud and talk about any forces that surprised anyone. Write each player's points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Was any force on the card that you did not think of? Which one?
flow.kid: Play the rounds. Bet with your force cards. Check the back of each card.
flow.parent: The cyclist card is the hardest. Let the children work out each arrow. The debate card is a talking point and not a quiz.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then ask: which card made you change your mind? Which force card did you play most? Why?
flow.say: Which thing had the most forces on it? Was any thing on a card without a force on it at all?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Say which card was the trickiest.
flow.parent: Do not mark any answer right on the debate card. Newton's and Einstein's descriptions are both used by physicists, and they predict the same orbit.
flow.think: Can you think of a thing that has no force on it at all?

experiments.title: The falling cones test: when does a falling thing stop speeding up?
experiments.question: A paper cone falls from your raised arm. Does it keep speeding up all the way down, or does it stop speeding up? And what happens to its speed if the cone is four times as heavy?
experiments.predict: Before you drop anything, guess. Four cones are pressed into each other and dropped beside one cone. Will the stack land in a quarter of the time, half the time or the same time? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Only the number of cones changes: one, two or four. The paper, the slope of the cones, the floor and the person dropping all stay the same. So does the starting height, with the tips level with a mark at 2 metres. The cone falls point down, with the fan off and the windows shut. Each load is dropped three times, because one drop can be spoiled by a draught or a wobble. The middle time of the three is used.

materials.item: 5 sheets of plain printer or notebook paper, about the same thickness
a round lid or small bowl about 16 centimetres across, to draw round
scissors, a pencil and a ruler
sticky tape
a phone with a stopwatch
a measuring tape or a metre ruler, and a bit of tape to mark a wall or door frame
a grown-up who can reach up to about 2 metres
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Circle the middle time of each load. Work out the speed over 2 metres for each load by dividing 2 by the middle time. Then write one sentence each for: what I think, what I saw and why.
experiments.context: In this investigation you drop paper cones from a measured height and time them, to find out whether a falling thing keeps speeding up. You also find out what changes when the thing gets heavier.

setup.art: Five paper circles with a slit cut to the middle, and one finished cone held in a hand with tape across the seam.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round a lid five times and cut out the circles. Cut a slit to the middle of each and tape each into a cone.

setup.art: A door frame with a tape mark at 2 metres, a tape measure running down it and a grown-up's raised hand holding a cone beside the mark.
setup.caption: 2. Stick a piece of tape on a wall or door frame exactly 2 metres above the floor. The grown-up holds the cones with the tips level with the tape.

setup.art: Three drops side by side: a single cone, a stack of two and a stack of four, each falling point down, and a child with a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. Drop one cone and time its fall three times. Then drop two cones pressed into each other, and then four, three times each.

flow.do: Draw round the lid on a sheet of paper five times and cut out the five circles. Cut one straight slit from the edge of each circle to its middle. Overlap the cut edges until the cone is about 12 centimetres across the open end. Check the open end with a ruler. Tape the seam in two places. Make all five cones in exactly the same way, so that they fit inside each other.
flow.say: We need five cones that are all the same. Why do you think we must make them the same?
flow.kid: Cut out five paper circles. Cut a slit to the middle of each one. Roll each into a cone and tape it. Make all five the same.
flow.parent: Cutting circles is fine for a child of 6 or more with blunt-ended scissors. Check that two cones pressed together fit snugly, with no gap at the sides. The cones must overlap by the same amount, or their slopes differ and the test is not fair.

flow.do: Measure 2 metres up from the floor on a wall or door frame and stick a piece of tape there. Clear the floor below. Switch off any fan and close the windows next to where you will drop. Then ask your child to make the prediction, and write it down.
flow.say: Four cones pressed into each other have four times the weight of one cone. Will the stack land in a quarter of the time, in half the time or in the same time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how long four cones will take to land compared with one cone. Write your guess and a reason.

ask.q: Why do you think heavy things might fall faster?
good: Because they are pulled harder by the Earth, so they should go quicker.
Because they are not blown about by the air as much.
Any honest reason is a good start.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say a quarter, because four times the weight should mean four times as fast. Others say the same time, because they have heard that heavy and light things fall together. Both guesses are worth testing, and the drops decide.

flow.do: The grown-up holds one cone, tip down, with the tip level with the 2 metre mark and the arm raised. The child holds the phone stopwatch. The grown-up says 'Go' as they open their fingers. The child starts the stopwatch at the word. The child stops it the moment the cone touches the floor. Write the time. Do this three times. A drop where the cone tumbles over or hits the wall does not count, so do that drop again.
flow.say: Watch the cone as it falls. Does it speed up all the way down, or does it settle at one speed? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Start the stopwatch when you hear 'Go'. Stop it when the cone touches the floor. Do it three times.

ask.q: Does the cone look as if it keeps speeding up, or does it seem to fall at one speed?
good: It seems to fall at one speed after the first moment.
It speeds up at the start and then looks steady.
Any honest answer. Looking is a hard way to tell, which is why we time it.

flow.parent: A single cone usually takes about 1.2 to 1.8 seconds to fall 2 metres. Never stand on a chair or stool to drop. If nobody can reach 2 metres, use a mark at 1.5 metres for every drop. All the times will then be shorter. Your fingers are slow at starting and stopping, but they are slow by about the same amount both times, so most of the error cancels. If the single cone lands in under 1 second, the paper is thick or the cones are small. Make new cones from thinner paper, such as a notebook sheet or a newspaper page, or use paper muffin cases. A short time is still usable, because we compare the loads with each other.

flow.do: Now drop two cones pressed into each other, and time three drops as before. Then do the same with four cones pressed into each other. Press them in firmly each time, so that they fall as one piece, point down. Write each time in the table.
flow.say: Before you time the stack of four, what do you think the time will be, compared with the single cone? Write it down. Then we will see.
flow.kid: Time two stacked cones three times, and then four stacked cones three times. Write each time.
flow.parent: Expect two stacked cones to take about three quarters of the single cone's time, and four stacked cones to take about 0.55 to 0.7 of it. These numbers come from a calculation, not from a family test, so your own may differ. If the four-stack lands in about a quarter of the single time, or in the same time as one, check two things. Were the cones pressed firmly into each other? Were the tips level with the mark? If your result is a little different, keep it and say so. A real result is better than a tidy one.

flow.do: Move the tape mark to 1 metre above the floor. Time one cone dropped from there, three times. Then work out how long the second metre took. Take the 1 metre middle time away from the 2 metre middle time.
flow.say: A stone dropped from 1 metre takes about half a second. Its second metre takes only about 0.2 seconds, because it keeps speeding up. How long did the second metre take for your cone?
flow.kid: Drop one cone from the 1 metre mark three times. Take the 1 metre time away from the 2 metre time.

ask.q: The second metre took the cone far longer than it would take a stone. What does that tell you about the push of the air?
good: The air is pushing up on the cone, and the push grows until it equals the pull of the Earth.
Something is holding the cone back, so it stops speeding up.

flow.parent: A single cone usually takes about 0.7 to 1.0 seconds from 1 metre, so the second metre takes about 0.5 to 0.8 seconds. That is only a little shorter than the first metre. A stone's second metre takes less than half as long as its first. So the cone is hardly speeding up in the second metre. It has reached a steady speed.

flow.do: Work out each speed by dividing 2 metres by the middle time. Look at the three speeds. Then write what you think, what you saw and why. End by saying what the test cannot tell us.
flow.say: Four cones had four times the weight. Did they fall four times as fast? Why do you think the air did this?
flow.kid: Divide 2 by each middle time. Which load was fastest? Write: what I think, what I saw, why.

ask.q: What would happen to the four cones if there were no air at all?
good: They would all land together, at the same moment, as the hammer and the feather did on the Moon.
Nothing would push back, so the cones would keep speeding up.

flow.parent: A calculation suggests results near 1.4 metres per second for one cone and near 2.3 for four stacked, and yours may differ. So four times the weight gave far less than four times the speed. The steady speed itself is about double. The average over 2 metres is lower, because the cone is still speeding up at the start. The reason is that the push of the air grows faster than the speed. Double the speed and the push grows about four times. So each stack stops speeding up when the push of the air equals its weight. A stack four times heavier needs twice the speed to do that. The test does not show why the push of air grows in this way, and it does not show what happens at much greater speeds. Ask what else the child would test: a bigger cone, a flatter cone, a different height.
flow.think: If you wanted a cone to fall more slowly still, what would you change, and why?

experiments.title: The scale under the book: how hard does a table push up?
experiments.question: A book rests on a scale and stays still. The Earth pulls it down. How hard does the scale push up, and does the push change if you press on the book?
experiments.predict: Before you press on the book, guess. If you press down on the book with your hand, will the scale read more, the same or less? And if you lift the book a little with your hand, will it read more, the same or less? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same scale, on the same flat table, and the same books are used each time. Only what your hand does changes: nothing, pressing down or lifting. The scale is set to zero with nothing on it at the start. Each reading is taken three times, because the numbers wobble a little.
results_table: Push in newtons (reading in kilograms times 10)

materials.item: a kitchen scale that reads in grams (or a bathroom scale, with a stack of books of at least 3 kilograms)
3 thick books or notebooks of different weights
a flat, firm table or floor
paper and a pencil

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out the push of the scale in newtons for each book by changing the reading to kilograms and multiplying by 10. Then write what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this investigation you use a scale as a force meter. You find out that a thing that is not moving still has a push from underneath. That push changes by exactly as much as your hand adds or takes away.

setup.art: A kitchen scale on a table with a display reading zero.
setup.caption: 1. Put the scale on a flat table and switch it on with nothing on it, so that it reads zero.

setup.art: A kitchen scale with a stack of two books on it and the display showing a number.
setup.caption: 2. Put one book in the middle of the scale. Write the reading. Then add a second book, and a third.

setup.art: A hand pressing down on the books on the scale, with a bigger number showing, and another with the hand lifting and a smaller number showing.
setup.caption: 3. Press down on the top book with your flat hand, and then lift it a little with your fingers under the edge. Watch the number change.

flow.do: Put the scale on a flat, firm table. Switch it on with nothing on it and wait until it reads zero. On a kitchen scale, press Tare if there is a Tare button. Do not lean on the table. Ask your child to say what the number means.
flow.say: The scale reads zero now. What do you think the scale is measuring when something is put on it?
flow.kid: Put the scale on the table and switch it on. It should say zero.
flow.parent: A kitchen scale has a platform that is squashed by a tiny amount when something is put on it. A sensor inside turns that squash into a number. Soft surfaces such as a bed or a carpet give wrong readings, so use a table or the floor. With a bathroom scale and no kitchen scale, use a stack of books of at least 3 kilograms, such as a school bag of books. Many bathroom scales are not accurate below 2 kilograms.

flow.do: Put the lightest book in the middle of the scale and write the reading. Add the next book and write the new reading. Then add the third. Change each reading to kilograms and multiply by 10 to get the push in newtons. For example, 600 grams is 0.6 kilograms, and 0.6 times 10 is 6 newtons.
flow.say: How hard do you think the Earth pulls on this book? And how hard is the scale pushing back? Are they the same, or different?
flow.kid: Put one book on the scale and write the number. Add the other books one at a time and write each number.

ask.q: The book is not moving. Is anything pushing on it?
good: Yes. The scale is pushing up, and the Earth is pulling down.
The two are equal, so the book stays still.

flow.parent: The reading in grams or kilograms shows how hard the scale is being squashed. The push of the scale on the book equals the book's weight. The weight in newtons is the reading in kilograms times about 10. A bathroom scale in kilograms works the same way. If the scale seems to read a little too much or too little, do not worry. What matters is that adding a book adds the same number to the reading as that book's weight.

flow.do: Leave all three books on the scale and wait until the reading is steady. Write it. Now press down on the top book with your flat hand and write the reading while you press. Then take your hand off and slide your fingers under the edge of the top book. Lift it very slightly, without taking it off the stack, and write the reading while you lift. Do each three times.
flow.say: You are pressing down on the books. Does the scale read more, the same or less? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Press down on the books and read the number. Then lift the top book a little and read the number again.

ask.q: The books did not move when you pressed. How can the scale read a bigger number?
good: The scale pushes up harder, as hard as the books' weight and your hand's push together.
The support force changes to match whatever is needed.

flow.parent: Pressing down adds your push to the weight, so the scale reads more, and the extra reading is your push. Lifting takes some of the weight off the scale, so it reads less. In both cases the push from the scale is exactly what is needed to hold the books still. If the reading barely changes, press harder, but never hard enough to bend the scale.

flow.do: If you have a bathroom scale, stand on it with your feet still and read the number. Bend your knees quickly, as if about to sit, and watch the number during the bend and just after. If the scale is digital and holds its reading, skip this and go on to the next step.
flow.say: When you bend your knees quickly, does the number go up or down for a moment? What do you think the floor is doing?
flow.kid: Stand on the scale. Bend your knees quickly. Watch the number.
flow.parent: On a scale that shows the number as it changes, the reading dips below your usual number for a moment as you start to drop. Then it rises above it as you stop. For that moment the floor pushes up with less than your weight, and you speed up downward. This is a small taste of what an astronaut feels all the time. Many digital scales are slow and freeze their number, so do not worry if nothing changes.

flow.do: Look at the table. Write one sentence each for what I think, what I saw and why. Finish with what the test cannot tell us.
flow.say: Nothing moved, yet the scale pushed. Why does a thing that is not moving need a push from underneath?
flow.kid: Write: what I think, what I saw, why. Then write one thing the scale cannot tell you.
flow.parent: The scale does not measure mass directly. It measures how hard its own top is pushed, and shows that as grams. On the Moon, the same books would give a lower reading, because the pull of the Moon is weaker. The mass of the books is the same. Ask your child what else they would test: a book on a soft mattress, or the same book in a lift.
flow.think: If the table pushed up with less than the book's weight, what would happen to the book?

experiments.title: How far can a magnet pull through cardboard?
experiments.question: A fridge magnet pulls a steel paper clip across a table without touching it. How thick a stack of card can sit in between before the pull is too weak to drag the clip along?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess how many millimetres of card the magnet can pull through. Will the pull fade away slowly as the card gets thicker, or will it hold well and then let go all at once? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same magnet, the same steel paper clip, the same smooth table and the same slow slide of the magnet are used every time. Only the number of card squares between the magnet and the clip changes. The squares are all cut from the same card. Each thickness is tried three times, because the magnet may slip. The answer is 'follows' only if the clip follows the magnet for at least 10 centimetres.

materials.item: a fridge magnet or any small magnet that sticks to the fridge
a steel paper clip (it should stick to a magnet)
cardboard from a cereal or biscuit box, cut into 20 squares about 5 centimetres each
scissors
a ruler with millimetres
a smooth, clear table
paper and a pencil

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write 'yes', 'sometimes' or 'no' for each try. Find the thickest stack where the clip still followed all three times, and the thinnest where it never followed. Then write what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this investigation you find out how the pull of a magnet fades as the gap grows. You test it by sliding the magnet over card and seeing when the clip below stops following.

setup.art: A cereal box being cut into squares, and a paper clip clinging to a fridge magnet.
setup.caption: 1. Cut 20 squares of thin card, about 5 centimetres each, and test that your paper clip sticks to the magnet.

setup.art: A paper clip on a table with a stack of card squares lying over it, held by a hand.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the clip on a smooth table. Put a stack of squares over it and hold the stack down with one hand.

setup.art: A magnet sliding over a stack of card with a dotted line showing a clip underneath following it, and a ruler beside the stack.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the magnet slowly along the top of the stack and watch whether the clip follows underneath. Add squares until it stops.

flow.do: Cut about 20 squares, 5 centimetres on each side, from thin card, such as a cereal box. Check the paper clip: it must stick to the magnet. If it does not, try another clip, because some clips are not steel. Stack the squares and measure the thickness of 10 of them with the ruler, then work out one square's thickness.
flow.say: The magnet pulls the clip even when it is not touching. How do you think the pull will change when there is more card in between?
flow.kid: Cut 20 squares from card. Check that the clip sticks to the magnet. Measure the stack of 10.
flow.parent: Thin card from a cereal box is about 0.5 millimetres, so 10 squares are about 5 millimetres. If your card is thicker, the thickness per square will be bigger, and that is fine as long as you measure the stack with the ruler. If you have a kitchen magnet that is very strong, it may hold the clip through all 20 squares. In that case use a notebook (about 5 millimetres) in place of squares.

flow.do: Ask your child to make the prediction, and write it down. Lay the clip flat on the smooth table.
flow.say: How many millimetres of card do you think the magnet can pull through? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the thickness at which the clip will stop following. Write your guess and a reason.

ask.q: Does the pull fade slowly or stop suddenly? What makes you say so?
good: It fades slowly, so the clip should follow up to a big thickness.
It lets go quickly, so only a thin stack will work.
Any honest reason is good.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children often guess by feeling. The test then tells them how good the feeling was.

flow.do: Start with no card. Slide the magnet slowly, about 10 centimetres, across the table beside the clip, and watch the clip follow. Now put 2 squares over the clip and hold them flat. Slide the magnet over the top of the stack, directly above the clip. Note if the clip follows for at least 10 centimetres. Add 2 squares at a time, and try three times at each thickness. Write 'yes', 'sometimes' or 'no'.
flow.say: At which stack does the clip start to be left behind? How can you tell that the pull is still there, even when the clip does not follow?
flow.kid: Slide the magnet over the stack. Does the clip follow? Add 2 squares and try again. Write what happens each time.

ask.q: What happens just before the clip stops following?
good: It follows a little and then falls behind.
It follows sometimes and sometimes not, which means the pull is just enough.

flow.parent: Slide the magnet slowly, about 2 centimetres each second, or the clip will be left behind even if the pull is strong. The clip may jump up and stick to the underside of the card, which is fine. Pull the magnet sideways at the same height each time. If a try is spoiled because the stack slipped, do that try again. Around the thickness where the clip begins to fail, 'sometimes' is a real and useful answer.

flow.do: Look at the table. Find the thickest stack where the clip followed all three times, and the thinnest where it never followed. Write what you think, what you saw and why. Finish with what the test cannot tell us.
flow.say: Was your guess close? How quickly did the pull fade as the card got thicker?
flow.kid: Find where the clip stopped following. Write: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.parent: Between 'follows every time' and 'never follows' there are often only a few squares, which is only a millimetre or two. This shows that the pull fades quickly with distance. The test tells us only whether the pull beat the grip of the table on the clip. It does not give the pull in newtons. To measure that we would need a spring that stretches, such as the one in a force meter. Ask your child what else they would test: a stronger magnet, two magnets stuck together, a heavier clip.
flow.think: If you had a magnet twice as strong, do you think it would pull through twice as many squares? How could you find out?

activities.title: Two questions on six things at home: draw the forces
activities.context: This activity teaches how to read the forces on any everyday thing. You ask two questions about six things in your home and draw an arrow for each force.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a school bag, a ceiling fan or a hanging light, a cup on a shelf, a fridge magnet on the fridge and a chair
a ruler

schedule.what: Find the forces on a bag, a fan, a cup, a magnet and a person, and draw a force diagram for two of them.

activities.record: Draw a box or dot for each thing, with one arrow for each force and a label on every arrow. Make the arrows for forces that balance the same length.

setup.art: A school bag on a wall hook with two question bubbles beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a thing, such as a school bag hanging on a hook. Ask: what is touching it? What is pulling it from a distance?

setup.art: A box on a page with an arrow down labelled Earth's pull and an arrow up labelled hook's pull.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the bag as a box. Draw one arrow for each force, starting at the box, with a label on each.

setup.art: Five small force diagrams in a row on a page, each with two or more labelled arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Do the same for a ceiling fan, a cup on a shelf, a fridge magnet on a fridge door and a person on a chair.

flow.do: Look at a school bag on a hook, or any hanging thing. Ask your child the two questions: what is touching the bag, and what is pulling it from a distance? Then draw the bag as a box on paper and add the two arrows. The hook pulls the bag up and the Earth pulls it down. Make the arrows the same length.
flow.say: What is touching the bag? What is pulling it without touching? What would happen if the hook let go?
flow.kid: Look at the bag. What is touching it? What is pulling it from far? Draw a box and two arrows.

ask.q: What is touching the bag?
good: The hook, and a little bit of the air.
The hook is the one that matters.

ask.q: What pulls it from a distance?
good: The Earth, through gravity.
Gravity pulls it down.

flow.parent: The air touches the bag too, but its push is so small that it does not count here. A force diagram shows the forces that matter. Both arrows are the same length because the bag is not speeding up or slowing down.

flow.do: Now do the same for four more things. First choose a fan or a hanging light. Then choose a cup on a shelf, your child on a chair and a fridge magnet on a door. For each one, ask the two questions and draw a box with arrows. The magnet is the hardest, because it has four forces. The Earth pulls it down and friction from the door holds it up. The magnetic pull draws it into the door, and the door pushes back out.
flow.say: Which forces do you think act on the fridge magnet? Why does it not slide down the door?
flow.kid: Draw a fan, a cup, a person and a magnet. Give each one arrows.

ask.q: Why does the magnet not slide down the fridge?
good: Friction between the magnet and the door holds it up.
The magnet pulls hard into the door, which makes the grip bigger.

flow.parent: The cup has gravity down and the support force from the shelf up. The fan has the pull of the rod up and gravity down. The person has gravity down and the chair's support force up. For the magnet, the magnetic pull in and the push of the door out are equal. Weight and friction are also equal. Praise any labelled arrow that is honest, even if a child finds only two of the four.

flow.do: Choose two of your drawings. Check that the arrows for forces that cancel are the same length. Then ask: which of the things you drew would fall if one force were switched off? Which force would you switch off?
flow.say: If you could switch off one force on the cup, which one would make the cup fall? What does that tell you about the table?
flow.kid: Pick two drawings. Check that the arrows that cancel are the same length. Which force would you switch off to make the thing fall?
flow.parent: The still things at home are all held still by forces in balance. Take your time and let your child say it in their own words.
flow.think: Can you find a thing in your home with no force on it at all?

activities.title: A pulley from a thread reel: two bottles that balance
activities.context: This activity shows that a rope carries the same pull all along it. You hang two equal bottles over a pulley and find how much extra water is needed to tip the balance.

materials.item: an empty thread reel, a tape roll or a plastic bangle, that turns freely
a round pencil or a thin steel rod that fits the reel
2 small plastic bottles of the same size, with thread loops tied round their necks
about 1 metre of strong thread or thin string
two stacks of books or two chair backs, a little apart
water, a teaspoon and a tray

schedule.what: Build the pulley, balance the bottles and find how much water tips the balance.

activities.record: Write the number of teaspoons of water that you needed to add before the bottle went down. Draw the pulley and put an arrow for the pull in the thread on each side.

setup.art: A thread reel on a pencil resting across two stacks of books on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Push the pencil through the reel. Rest the two ends of the pencil on two stacks of books, so that the reel can turn freely in between.

setup.art: Two bottles hanging from a thread that runs over a reel, above a tray.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a bottle at each end of a long thread laid over the reel. Both bottles hang freely, a hand's width above a tray.

setup.art: A hand with a teaspoon pouring water into the right-hand bottle that has begun to sink.
setup.caption: 3. Add water to one bottle, one teaspoon at a time, until it goes down.

flow.do: Push the pencil through the reel. Lay the pencil across two stacks of books, or the backs of two chairs. The reel should hang in the gap and turn freely. Tie a loop of thread round the neck of each bottle. Join the two loops with a long thread laid over the reel. Fill both bottles with water to the same level. Put a tray on the floor below.
flow.say: The thread goes over a wheel. What do you think the wheel does to the pull in the thread?
flow.kid: Push a pencil through a thread reel. Lay it across two stacks of books. Hang a bottle on each side of the thread over the reel.
flow.parent: A grown-up should check that the stacks are steady and the pencil cannot slip off. The bottles are plastic, so nothing can break. If the thread keeps slipping off the reel, tie a small piece of tape across the groove.

flow.do: Lift one bottle a hand's width higher than the other and let go. See if the bottles stay where they are. They should stay still because the pull on each side is the same. Then ask your child how big the pull in the thread is on each side. They can use what they know about gravity and weight.
flow.say: Both bottles are the same. The Earth pulls each one down. What is pulling each bottle up? How strong is that pull, compared with the weight of one bottle?
flow.kid: Let go of the bottles. Do they move? Why do they stay still?

ask.q: The thread goes over a reel. Is the pull in the thread the same on both sides?
good: Yes, because the bottles are the same and neither moves.
The reel changes only the direction, not the size, of the pull.

flow.parent: Each bottle is held by the pull of the thread, which equals the bottle's weight. The same thread carries the same pull on both sides, so the bottles balance. The reel only changes the direction of the pull. A small amount of friction in the reel helps the bottles stay in place.

flow.do: Add one teaspoon of water to one bottle, then another, then count the teaspoons. Stop as soon as that bottle starts to go down. Write the number. Do it again on the other bottle.
flow.say: Why does it take a few teaspoons before the bottle goes down? What is the reel doing against you?
flow.kid: Add water, a teaspoon at a time, to one bottle. Count the spoons. Stop when it goes down.

ask.q: Which direction is friction pointing when the bottle starts to sink?
good: Against the sinking, so upward on the thread.
Friction opposes the motion.

flow.parent: The extra weight needed is the friction in the reel and the stiffness of the thread. A reel that turns very freely needs only one or two teaspoons. A thread that rubs needs many. Each teaspoon is about 5 grams, which is about one twentieth of a newton, so even a pulling difference that small can show.

flow.do: Now pull one side of the thread down with your hand. The other bottle rises, as a bucket does at a well. Then pour the water onto a plant and dry the tray.
flow.say: At a well you pull the rope down to bring the bucket up. How does the pulley let you do that?
flow.kid: Pull one side of the thread down. The other bottle goes up. Pour the water onto a plant.
flow.parent: The reel turns the pull around. Pulling down on one side gives a pull up on the other. It is easier for a person to pull down, because the body's weight helps.
flow.think: Why do you think people pull a rope down at a well, and not up?

activities.title: Feel the water push up: floating, sinking and a steel katori
activities.context: This activity lets you feel upthrust with your own hands. You push an empty bottle under water, float a steel katori and find how many coins it carries before it sinks.

materials.item: a bucket or a large steel or plastic basin, half full of water
a tray or a towel for the floor
an empty plastic bottle with its cap on
a steel katori or small bowl
30 identical coins, such as 1 rupee coins (or rice and a teaspoon)
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Push a bottle under water, float a katori, add coins and find the load at which it sinks.

activities.record: Write how many coins the katori held before it sank, and how that number changes if the katori is set down tilted or pushed under water. Draw the two arrows on the floating katori.

setup.art: A hand pushing a capped plastic bottle down in a basin of water, with an arrow pointing up.
setup.caption: 1. Put the basin on a tray on the floor. Push an empty capped bottle slowly down into the water and feel the push on your hand.

setup.art: A steel katori floating on water, open end up.
setup.caption: 2. Set the steel katori on the water, open end up, and let go gently. It floats.

setup.art: A katori nearly full of coins sitting low in the water, with a hand adding another.
setup.caption: 3. Add coins one at a time, gently into the middle, until the katori sinks. Count them.

flow.do: Put the basin on a tray on the floor and fill it half full of water. Push the empty, capped bottle slowly down into the water, and notice how hard the water pushes back up. Ask your child to push it all the way to the bottom. Let go and watch what happens.
flow.say: How hard do you have to push the bottle down? What is pushing back? Why does the bottle shoot up when you let go?
flow.kid: Push the empty bottle down in the water. Feel the push back. Let go.
flow.parent: The push you feel is upthrust. The deeper the bottle goes, the more water it pushes aside, until it is fully under, and from then on the push stays about the same. If the bottle shoots up and splashes, it is working. A towel under the basin helps.

flow.do: Set the steel katori gently on the water, open end up. Let go. It floats. Then push it under, open end down, so that it traps air. Feel the push. Then tip it so that it fills with water and watch it sink.
flow.say: A steel katori is heavier than water, and yet it floats. Why do you think it floats when set down gently?
flow.kid: Set the katori on the water. Let go. Now push it down and feel it push back.

ask.q: Why does the katori float when set down, and sink when full of water?
good: When it is full of water it no longer pushes aside enough water to equal its weight.
A hollow shape pushes away more water than a lump of the same steel.

flow.parent: The katori floats because its hollow shape pushes aside a lot of water. The weight of that water equals the katori's weight. A solid lump of steel the same weight pushes aside much less, and sinks. Many steel katoris are slightly different. If yours sinks when set down gently, use a wider bowl.

flow.do: Float the empty katori. Add coins one at a time, gently, near the middle. Count each coin. Stop when the katori sinks and write the number. Do it three times and use the middle number. Most katoris carry between 10 and 30 coins. If you run out of coins, use level teaspoons of rice, in a small pile in the middle, and count the teaspoons.
flow.say: How many coins do you think it can carry before it sinks? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Float the katori. Add coins one at a time. Count them. Write the number when it sinks.

ask.q: What changed each time you added a coin?
good: The katori went lower, so it pushed aside more water.
The weight went up and the upthrust went up to match, until it could not.

flow.parent: More coins push the katori deeper, so it pushes aside more water, and the upthrust grows. It grows until the katori is nearly full or the water spills over the edge. Then no more water can be pushed aside, and it sinks. The number of coins depends on the size of the katori, so every family will get a different number.

flow.do: Take out the coins and dry them, and pour the water onto a plant. Wipe the tray.
flow.say: A ship is made of steel and floats. What does the katori tell you about why?
flow.kid: Dry the coins. Pour the water on a plant.
flow.parent: A ship works in the way the katori does: a hollow shape that pushes aside a very large weight of water.
flow.think: How could you make the katori carry more coins without changing its size?

activities.title: The coin see-saw: where a small weight balances a big one
activities.context: This activity shows how a lever works. You balance coins on a ruler resting on a pencil and find the rule for where to put them.

materials.item: a 30 centimetre plastic or wooden ruler
a round pencil
8 identical coins, such as 1 rupee coins
a smooth table
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Balance the ruler on the pencil, place coins at different distances and find the rule for balance.

activities.record: Fill in a table with columns: coins on the left, distance on the left, coins on the right, distance on the right, balanced or not. Write the rule you find.

setup.art: A ruler balanced on a round pencil on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the pencil across the table. Rest the ruler on the pencil at its 15 centimetre mark so that it balances.

setup.art: A ruler on a pencil with two coins near one end and one coin at the right distance on the other side.
setup.caption: 2. Put two coins on the 5 centimetre mark. Then put one coin on the other side and find where it balances.

setup.art: A table in a notebook with coins and distances written in.
setup.caption: 3. Try other numbers of coins and write down each place where the ruler balances.

flow.do: Lay the pencil on a smooth table. Rest the ruler across the pencil with the 15 centimetre mark over it. Move the ruler a little until it balances flat. If the pencil rolls, put a small piece of tape under it or put it in a groove made by two books.
flow.say: A see-saw balances when the weights on both sides are equal, and are the same distance from the middle. What do you think will happen if we put 2 coins on one side and 1 coin on the other?
flow.kid: Put the ruler across the pencil so that it balances. Mark the middle.
flow.parent: The pencil is the pivot. The ruler is the lever.

flow.do: Put 2 coins on the ruler at the 10 centimetre mark, which is 5 centimetres from the pivot. Place 1 coin on the other side and slide it until the ruler is level. Write its distance from the pivot. Then do the same with 3 coins at 5 centimetres from the pivot, and 1 coin on the other side. Then try 1 coin at 10 centimetres from the pivot, and 2 coins on the other side. Write every result in the table.
flow.say: Where do you think the single coin must go to balance the two coins? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put 2 coins near the pivot. Slide 1 coin on the other side until the ruler is level. Write where it is.

ask.q: The single coin had to go farther from the pivot. Why?
good: It is lighter, so it must be farther out to balance the heavier side.
A small weight far away balances a big weight near.
Number of coins times distance is the same on both sides.

flow.parent: Two coins 5 centimetres from the pivot are balanced by one coin 10 centimetres from the pivot on the other side. Three coins at 5 centimetres are balanced by one coin at 15 centimetres, which is the very end of the ruler. Count the coins times the distance on each side, and compare. If a result is a little off, the ruler may not be balanced on its own, or the coins may be different. Results within about 1 centimetre are good.

flow.do: Look at the table. Find the rule. Then link it to a door: push at the handle and push near the hinge. Which is easier, and why?
flow.say: A door is a lever whose pivot is the hinge. Why is it hard to push a door near the hinge?
flow.kid: Find the rule for the coins. Then push a door near the hinge and at the handle.
flow.parent: The rule is: the number of coins times their distance from the pivot is equal on both sides. A big push close to the pivot balances a small push far from it. The big fishing nets in Kochi use this rule, and so does your arm.
flow.think: Where is the pivot in your arm, and where is the push?

activities.title: Find the lever in your own arm
activities.context: This activity shows how your arm works as a lever. You measure two distances along your forearm and work out how much harder your muscle pulls than the load weighs.

materials.item: a ruler or a tape measure
a 1 litre bottle of water
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Feel the biceps pull, measure the two distances and work out the ratio.

activities.record: Write the two distances in centimetres, divide the longer by the shorter, and write the answer with the words 'about this many times'.

setup.art: A child sitting with the elbow on a table, a hand on the front of the upper arm.
setup.caption: 1. Sit with your elbow on a table and your forearm upright. Put your other hand on the front of your upper arm.

setup.art: A child holding a water bottle with the forearm raised, one hand feeling the upper arm bulge.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a 1 litre bottle and bend your arm. Feel the muscle bulge under your hand.

setup.art: A tape measure running along a forearm from the elbow to the palm, with a short mark near the elbow.
setup.caption: 3. Measure from the elbow's pointed bone to your palm. Then measure from the elbow to the place where the biceps joins the forearm. You find it by feeling the cord inside the elbow.

flow.do: Sit with your elbow on the table and your forearm upright. Put the other hand over the front of the upper arm. Pick up the 1 litre bottle in the hand, and slowly bend the arm, bringing the bottle towards your shoulder. Feel the biceps bulge and harden. Then straighten the arm, and feel the biceps soften and the muscle at the back of the arm go hard.
flow.say: Which muscle works when the arm bends? Which works when the arm straightens? Can a muscle push?
flow.kid: Bend your arm with the bottle and feel the front muscle go hard. Straighten it and feel the back muscle go hard.

ask.q: Why does the arm need a muscle at the back as well as the front?
good: A muscle can only pull, so one muscle pulls the arm up and another pulls it down.
They work as a pair, pulling in opposite directions.

flow.parent: A muscle can only pull. So the arm needs one muscle on the front to bend it and one on the back to straighten it. The bottle weighs about 10 newtons.

flow.do: Measure from the pointed bone of your elbow to the middle of your palm, along the forearm. This is the distance from the pivot to the load. Now feel the inside of your elbow. About 3 to 5 centimetres below the elbow joint, you can feel a firm cord. That is where the biceps joins the forearm. Measure from the elbow's pointed bone to that spot.
flow.say: The bottle is far from the elbow. The muscle joins very close to the elbow. Which do you think has to pull harder, the muscle or the load? Why?
flow.kid: Measure the elbow to the palm. Then measure the elbow to the place where the biceps joins. Write both.

ask.q: Divide the long distance by the short one. What does the answer tell you?
good: The muscle pulls that many times harder than the load weighs.
A big ratio means the muscle works very hard for a small load.

flow.parent: The two numbers for a child of 8 to 10 are usually about 20 to 25 centimetres and about 3 to 4 centimetres. The ratio is then about 5 to 8. The attachment point is hard to find exactly, so use the range, not one number. The biceps pulls about this many times as hard as the load weighs.

flow.do: Look at the ratio. If the bottle weighs 10 newtons, how hard is your biceps pulling? Then ask what the body gains from this odd arrangement.
flow.say: Your muscle pulls many times harder than the bottle weighs. What does your hand gain in return?
flow.kid: Multiply 10 newtons by your ratio. That is the pull of your biceps.
flow.parent: What the arm gives up in strength, it gains in range and quickness. This is why a bowler can send a cricket ball so fast.
flow.think: Would you prefer a muscle that pulls less hard and an arm that swings less far? Why?

activities.title: Which surface grips? The tilted board test
activities.context: This activity compares friction on different surfaces. You tilt a board slowly and find how steep it must be before a rubber eraser slides.

materials.item: a hardback book or a stiff board about 30 centimetres long
a rubber eraser
a sheet of paper, a piece of cloth and a plastic bag, each big enough to cover the board
sticky tape
a ruler
a few drops of water
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Tilt a board covered with four surfaces and measure the height at which the eraser starts to slide.

activities.record: Write the height of the raised end in centimetres at which the eraser started to slide on each surface. Put the surfaces in order, from the one that gripped most to the one that gripped least.

setup.art: A hardback book flat on a table with an eraser on it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the book flat on a table with one short end at the table edge. Put the eraser near the middle.

setup.art: A hand lifting one end of a book, with a ruler held upright under it and the eraser starting to slide.
setup.caption: 2. Lift the end of the book slowly. Stop the moment the eraser starts to slide, and measure how high the end is.

setup.art: Four copies of the same tilted book, each with a different surface laid on it.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the book with paper, cloth and a plastic bag in turn, taped flat. Test each one.

flow.do: Lay the book flat with its spine away from you. Put the eraser in the middle of the cover, with its long side across the slope. Raise the end nearest you very slowly with one hand, and keep the other end touching the table. Stop the instant the eraser begins to slide, and hold the book still. Measure the height of the raised end above the table.
flow.say: What do you think is stopping the eraser from sliding down? In which direction does it point?
flow.kid: Lift one end of the book slowly. Stop the moment the eraser slides. Measure the height.
flow.parent: Friction points up the slope, against the sliding. It holds the eraser until the slope is steep enough that gravity along the slope is bigger than friction. Lift at the same slow speed each time, and always put the eraser in the same place, with the same side down.

flow.do: Tape a sheet of paper flat over the cover and test again, three times. Do the same with cloth and with the plastic bag. Lastly, put the plastic bag on again and add three drops of water to it, spread with a finger. Test again three times. Write the heights and use the middle of the three for each surface.
flow.say: Which surface do you think will grip the eraser the most? Which the least? Why?
flow.kid: Test the eraser on paper, on cloth and on plastic. Then try plastic with water. Write each height.

ask.q: Which surface gave the highest slope before sliding, and what does that mean?
good: The one with the most friction, because it held the eraser on the steepest slope.
More grip needs a steeper slope to beat it.

flow.parent: The wet plastic usually grips least. Every board and eraser is different, so only compare the surfaces on your own board with each other. If the eraser never slides, even when the board is almost upright, use a smooth plastic ruler or a steel spoon instead of the eraser.

flow.do: Put the surfaces in order. Then draw a force diagram for the eraser just before it slides: gravity down, the board pushing out from its surface and friction up the slope. Ask what the diagram says when the eraser starts to slide.
flow.say: Where have you seen a smooth surface that is slippery and a rough surface that grips? Which would you want on a bathroom floor?
flow.kid: Put the surfaces in order. Draw the eraser with three arrows.
flow.parent: Friction does not slow things only. It also lets a walker push off the ground, and a tyre grip the road. On a slope, friction is what holds a standing person still.
flow.think: What could you put on the board to make the eraser slide at a much lower slope?

activities.title: A rubbed balloon and torn paper: the static pull on a dry day
activities.context: This activity lets you meet the electric force. You rub a balloon and see it pull tiny paper bits without touching them. It works best on a dry day, and a failure tells you something too.

materials.item: a balloon, blown up
a woollen or synthetic cloth, or dry hair
a sheet of paper torn into about 20 tiny bits
a plastic comb or ruler

schedule.what: Rub a balloon on dry hair or wool, hold it over paper bits and see if they jump. Then try a wall.

activities.record: Write what happened on the day you tried it, and whether the air in the room was dry or damp. Draw the balloon, the paper bits and an arrow of pull.

setup.art: A table with a scatter of tiny paper bits.
setup.caption: 1. Tear a sheet of paper into about 20 tiny bits and spread them on a table.

setup.art: A balloon held above the paper, with some bits leaping up to it.
setup.caption: 2. Rub the balloon on dry hair or wool 20 times, then hold it about 2 centimetres above the paper.

setup.art: A balloon sticking to a wall with small plus and minus signs along the touching place.
setup.caption: 3. Press the rubbed balloon on a wall and let go. See how long it stays.

flow.do: Spread the paper bits on a table. Rub the balloon against dry hair or a woollen or synthetic cloth about 20 times, always in the same direction. Slowly hold the balloon about 2 centimetres above the bits and watch.
flow.say: The balloon will not touch the paper. Do you think anything will happen? What would you try if nothing does?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon on dry hair 20 times. Hold it over the paper. Watch.
flow.parent: This works well on a dry cool day and badly on a damp, hot day, because damp air lets the charge leak away. If nothing happens, rub for longer, use a different cloth, or try a plastic comb through dry hair. If it still does not work, that is a real result.

flow.do: Rub the balloon again and hold it against a wall, or a door, and let go. Rub two balloons and bring them near each other, hanging from threads. Watch whether they come together or push apart.
flow.say: Did the paper jump to the balloon, or did the balloon pull the paper? Which pulled which?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon and press it on the wall. Does it stay? Hang two rubbed balloons beside each other.

ask.q: Why do the two rubbed balloons push each other apart?
good: They carry the same kind of charge, and the same kinds push apart.
Like charges repel.

flow.parent: Rubbing moves tiny particles called electrons from the hair or cloth onto the balloon. The balloon now has extra electric charge, which pulls on light things nearby. Two balloons rubbed the same way push each other apart, because they carry the same kind of charge. The paper also pulls on the balloon, just as hard.

flow.do: Look at what happened and write one line about the day: dry or damp air, and how long the balloon stayed on the wall.
flow.say: What do you think changes when the air is damp? Where could the charge be going?
flow.kid: Write how the day was and what happened.
flow.parent: The electric force is much stronger than gravity. A small rubbed balloon lifts a bit of paper against the pull of the whole Earth.
flow.think: If a balloon can pull a bit of paper up against the whole Earth, what does that say about how strong the electric force is?

projects.title: A week of forces: a force-diagram notebook of home, street and school
projects.context: In this project you spend five days finding the forces on everyday things in different places and drawing them. By the end you have a small notebook of force diagrams and a list of the forces you could not explain.

materials.item: a notebook or folded sheets of paper
a pencil and a ruler
a phone camera (optional)

schedule.what: In the kitchen, draw the forces on a pot on a shelf, a lid on a jar and a spoon in a katori.
On a bus, a bicycle or a walk, draw the forces on a person standing and on a moving wheel.
With your school bag, draw the forces on the bag on a hook, on your back and held out at arm's length.
At a play space or a festival, draw the forces on a swing, a kite or a swaying lantern.
Pick the four best drawings, check each arrow, and write one question you could not answer.

projects.record: A notebook with one force diagram on each page. Each arrow has a label of what is pushing or pulling. Each page has a line saying whether the forces are balanced and how you know. Add a page of questions that you could not answer.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded and stapled into a small notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Fold three sheets of paper in half to make a small notebook.

setup.art: A child pointing at a pot on a stove with two question bubbles beside it.
setup.caption: 2. On each day, choose three things in the place you are in. For each, ask: what is touching it, and what pulls it from far?

setup.art: A page with three boxes, each with labelled arrows and a note below.
setup.caption: 3. Draw each as a box with arrows. Check the lengths. Write if the forces are balanced.

flow.do: Day 1, in the kitchen. Choose three things: a steel pot on a shelf, a lid on a jar and a spoon resting in a katori. For each one, ask the two questions, and draw a box with arrows. Write below it whether the forces are balanced, and how you can tell. The spoon is the hardest, because it touches the katori in two places.
flow.say: What is touching the pot? What is pulling it from a distance? Are the forces balanced? How do you know?
flow.kid: Draw a pot, a lid and a spoon with arrows. Write balanced or not balanced under each.
flow.parent: The pot has weight down and the support force of the shelf up. It is still, so they balance. The lid has weight, the jar's push up, and the push of the air. A leaning spoon has weight, a support force at the katori's rim and another at the katori's bottom, and friction. Do not worry if a child finds only some of them.

flow.do: Day 2, on a bus, a bicycle or a walk. Choose a person standing on the bus, a bicycle wheel and a bag on a lap. Draw the forces on each. For the person standing in a bus that is braking, ask: what is the floor doing now? Which way does friction point on the wheel when the bicycle speeds up?
flow.say: When the bus brakes and you lean forward, what do you think is happening to the forces on you?
flow.kid: Draw a standing person, a wheel and a bag. Add arrows for each.
flow.parent: On a bus that moves steadily, a standing person has weight down and the floor's push up. When the bus brakes, the floor pushes backward on the feet through friction, and the body tends to keep going. On a bicycle's driving wheel, friction from the road points forward. Draw this from a seat or from memory, never while standing on a moving bus.

flow.do: Day 3, with your school bag. Draw the bag hanging on a hook. Draw the bag on your back as you stand. Draw it held out at arm's length. Ask which arrows are the same in the three drawings and which are different.
flow.say: In which of the three pictures does your body work hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the bag three ways. Write which one makes your arm tired.
flow.parent: In all three the bag has weight down. What changes is who or what pulls up: the hook, the straps pulling on the shoulders or the muscles of the arm.

flow.do: Day 4, at a play space or at a festival, or at home from a picture or a memory. Draw the forces on a swing at its highest point and at the bottom, on a kite and on a swaying lantern. Use arrows of different lengths. Draw only from where you stand on the ground.
flow.say: At which point on the swing do you think the rope pulls hardest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a swing, a kite or a lantern, with arrows. Make the longest arrow for the biggest force.
flow.parent: At the bottom of a swing the rope must pull up harder than the weight, because it is also turning the swing round. A kite has the string's pull, weight and the push of the wind. A lantern has weight down and tension up.

flow.do: Day 5. Pick the four best drawings. Check each arrow: does it start on the thing, point the way the force acts and carry a label? Where forces cancel, are the arrows the same length? Then write one question that you could not answer.
flow.say: Which drawing was hardest? What force were you unsure about?
flow.kid: Check four drawings. Write one question you could not answer.
flow.parent: A good notebook has honest labels and one honest question. A question may be as big as 'what is a force?'.
flow.think: Is there anything on your pages that has no force on it at all?

projects.title: Which way is down for a root? Moong sprouts turned on their side
projects.context: In this project you grow moong sprouts, turn them on their side and watch the roots bend towards the pull of the Earth. You see how a living being reads a force.

materials.item: 3 tablespoons of whole moong seeds
a clear plastic cup or a small clear jar
kitchen tissue or a clean cloth
a marker pen
a ruler with millimetres
a tray or plate
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: In the evening, soak the moong seeds in water.
Press 6 seeds between damp tissue and the wall of the cup, with the pointed ends down.
When roots are 1 centimetre long, mark them on the cup, then lay the cup on its side.
Look at the roots and see how they have bent. Measure the bend.
Turn the cup upside down, and mark where the roots point.
Draw all three positions and write what you think the roots are doing.

projects.record: Draw the cup on days 3, 4 and 6 with the roots as they look. Write which way the roots pointed, and how long they took to turn.

setup.art: A steel bowl of moong seeds under water.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: soak the moong seeds overnight.

setup.art: A clear cup with tissue inside and six seeds pressed against the clear wall.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: line a cup with damp tissue and press the seeds between the tissue and the cup, with the pointed ends down.

setup.art: A cup lying on its side, with roots drawn on the glass and some now curving downward.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: draw round each root on the cup with a pen, then lay the cup on its side and see which way the roots grow.

flow.do: In the evening, put 3 tablespoons of moong seeds in a bowl and cover them with water by about two finger-widths. Leave them for 8 to 10 hours.
flow.say: Seeds are alive. When they drink, they wake. Where do you think the root will grow from, and which way will it grow?
flow.kid: Soak the seeds in water. They need to drink overnight.
flow.parent: Use whole green moong, not split. Old seeds may not sprout, so soak a few more than you need. The seeds swell as they drink.

flow.do: Drain the seeds. Line a clear cup with a strip of damp kitchen tissue, folded to fit round the inside. Press 6 swollen seeds between the tissue and the clear wall of the cup, spaced apart. Put the pointed end of each seed down. Put a little water in the bottom of the cup, about one finger-width. Keep the cup upright, in a warm place away from direct sun. Check the tissue is damp every day.
flow.say: Which way do you think the root will come out, up or down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Press 6 seeds between the tissue and the cup wall. Keep a little water in the bottom.
flow.parent: In cool weather keep the cup in the warmest room of the house, never over a flame. Many seeds will show a small white root by the next day. If no root shows by the morning of day 3, wait one more day, because cold slows sprouting. If a seed grows a white fuzz, remove that seed and rinse the rest. Use plastic, not glass, if a child may knock it.

flow.do: Look at the roots. Choose the 4 that have grown about 1 centimetre. On the outside of the cup, draw round each root with a marker pen, and write the date. Then lay the cup gently on its side, with the wall that holds the seeds facing you. The roots now point sideways, and you can still see them. Keep the tissue damp, and put the cup on a tray.
flow.say: The roots now point sideways. What do you think they will do? What will tell you that they have sensed something?
flow.kid: Mark each root on the cup with a pen. Then lay the cup on its side.
flow.parent: Roots usually curve down within 6 to 24 hours. Some of the seeds may not do it, which is normal. Count only the ones that grew. The root tip senses gravity with tiny heavy grains inside its cells that settle to the lower side.

flow.do: Look at the roots. Draw round their new positions with a pen of a different colour. See which way each root now points, and measure with the ruler how far the tip has moved from its earlier line. Write the angle: more or less than a right angle.
flow.say: Which way did the roots bend? How did the root know where down is?
flow.kid: Draw round the new root positions with a different pen. Which way did they bend?

ask.q: How can a root know which way is down, with no eyes?
good: The root cells feel the pull of the Earth through tiny heavy grains inside them.
They sense gravity, and then they choose where to grow.

flow.parent: Most roots bend downward, back towards the pull of the Earth, though some wander. The bend happens just behind the tip. The roots are not pulled down. They choose to grow in a curve, by growing faster on the upper side.

flow.do: Stand the cup upright again, with the wall that holds the seeds still facing you. The roots that bent now point sideways. Mark their tips with a pen of a third colour. Leave the cup for a few hours, or until the next morning. Then draw round their new positions.
flow.say: The roots have been turned again. What do you think they will do this time? What does this tell you about the root's job?
flow.kid: Stand the cup upright. Mark the root tips. Look again later.
flow.parent: The roots should again turn downward, towards the pull of the Earth. If your seeds do not respond, that is a real result, and you can say so.

flow.do: Draw the cup three times, showing the roots on day 3, day 4 and day 6. Write one sentence each for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask whether the root decided to turn, or was only moved.
flow.say: Is the root deciding where to grow, or being moved? What would you test to find out?
flow.kid: Draw the three positions. Write what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.parent: Some scientists say a root is a being that senses and chooses where to grow. Others say it is a chain of automatic responses. The root's response cannot be predicted from gravity alone, because the root also responds to water and light. Wash the cup, and plant the sprouts in a pot if you like.
flow.think: If you could ask the root why it bent, what do you think it would say?

challenges.title: A paper bridge that holds a cup of coins
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a bridge from two sheets of paper across a gap, and find how much weight it can carry.
challenges.problem: Build a bridge across a gap of 20 centimetres between two stacks of books, using only 2 sheets of paper and sticky tape. The winner carries the most coins in a small cup at the middle. There is more than one good way to do it.
constraints: Use only 2 sheets of paper and up to 1 metre of tape. Nothing else may be part of the bridge.
The bridge rests on the two stacks of books and is not taped to them.
The gap is 20 centimetres, measured between the stacks.
Load the bridge by adding coins one at a time to a small paper cup that sits at the middle. Stop when the bridge sags down or collapses.
Test each design twice and write both counts.
materials: two stacks of books of the same height
a small paper cup or a plastic katori

setup.art: A flat sheet of paper across a gap between two stacks of books with a small cup in the middle, sagging.
setup.caption: 1. Make a 20 centimetre gap between two stacks of books and lay one flat sheet across it. Put the cup in the middle.

setup.art: A cup of coins pressing the paper down in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Add coins to the cup one at a time until the paper sags too much. Write the number.

setup.art: Three bridges side by side: a flat sheet, a folded concertina and a tube.
setup.caption: 3. Change the paper's shape and try again. Write the number each time.

flow.do: Make two stacks of books about 20 centimetres apart. Lay one flat sheet of paper across the gap, the long way. About 5 centimetres of paper should rest on each stack. Put the empty cup on the middle of the paper. Add coins one at a time until the paper sags to touch the table or tips off. Write the number of coins. This is your first bridge, and every other bridge is compared with it.
flow.say: A flat sheet is weak. Where do you think the paper is pulled and where is it squashed when a weight is on it?
flow.kid: Lay one sheet across the gap. Add coins to the cup until it sags. Write the number.
flow.parent: Most flat sheets carry between none and three coins. Under a load, the top of the paper is squeezed and the bottom is stretched. A bridge must carry both.

flow.do: Try the usual solutions. Fold the sheet like a concertina, with folds about 1.5 centimetres wide, so that it has ridges along its length. Or roll the sheet into a tube and tape the seam. Or fold it in thirds along its length to make a U-shape. Test each one with coins, twice, and write the numbers.
flow.say: Which of these shapes do you think will carry the most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fold the sheet into a concertina, a tube and a U-shape. Test each with coins.

ask.q: Why does a folded sheet carry more than a flat one made of the same paper?
good: The folds make it taller, so it bends much less.
The fold turns bending into stretching and squashing along the paper.

flow.parent: A flat sheet bends easily. A fold or a tube makes the paper stand up, so that the stretching and squashing are spread over a taller shape. A concertina often carries 10 or more coins, many more than the flat sheet. A tube may carry more, but it may flatten if the seam opens. Your numbers will differ.

flow.do: Now try the creative solutions. Use the second sheet too. Tape a flat sheet under a concertina to make a box shape. Or bend the paper into an arch that pushes outward on the book stacks. Or roll small tubes and tape them side by side. Test each design twice. Write the number each time and draw the bridge.
flow.say: What is the arch doing to the book stacks? Why do the stacks have to stay put?
flow.kid: Use the second sheet. Make a stronger bridge. Test it. Draw it.

ask.q: Where does the weight of the coins finally go?
good: Through the bridge to the books, then to the table, then to the ground.
Every part passes the push on, down to the ground.

flow.parent: An arch carries a load by pushing outward at its feet. If the stacks slide apart, the arch flattens. The books must stay in place, which means the ground must push back on the arch, as it does for a real stone bridge. Real bridges are made like this too. The Howrah Bridge's arms and the cables of the Bandra-Worli Sea Link each carry the load in a different way.

flow.do: Compare all your designs. Which carried the most coins for the same two sheets? Which was the lightest? Which would you trust if people walked over it? Answer in one sentence each.
flow.say: Was the best design the one you expected? Is there a design you did not try that might beat them all?
flow.kid: Pick the best bridge. Write why you think it won.
flow.parent: There is no single best bridge, only the best for a given job. A bridge for a heavy lorry is different from one for people on foot.
flow.think: If you could use a tiny bit of glue, where would you put it to make the bridge stronger?

general: Fold the sheet into a concertina so that it has ridges along its length.
Roll the sheet into a tube and tape the seam.
Fold the long edges up into a U-shaped trough.
creative: Tape a flat sheet under a concertina to make a hollow box shape, like a bridge deck.
Bend the paper into an arch and keep the feet from sliding apart by taping a paper string between them.
Roll several thin tubes and tape them side by side like bamboo poles.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own bridge from the same two sheets of paper and test it. What made it carry more than a flat sheet? Is the strongest bridge the same as the best bridge?

challenges.title: A parachute that makes a coin fall slowly
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge about air resistance. You make a parachute from a plastic bag so that a coin takes the longest time to fall from a measured height.
challenges.problem: Make a parachute that carries a 5 rupee coin, or any small coin, from a height of 2 metres to the floor. Make the fall last as long as you can. There is more than one good way to do it.
constraints: Use a plastic bag or a light cloth, thread, tape and scissors. The only load is the coin.
Drop from a raised arm, with the load tip level with a mark 2 metres above the floor.
Time each drop with a phone stopwatch. Drop three times and use the middle time.
Compare your parachute with a plain coin dropped from the same height.
materials: a plastic bag or a light cotton cloth
4 pieces of thread, each about 25 centimetres
a measuring tape and tape to mark 2 metres on a wall

setup.art: A square of plastic bag with a thread at each corner joined below to a coin.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a square of plastic about 30 centimetres on each side. Tape a thread to each corner and tie the four threads to a coin.

setup.art: A raised arm holding a parachute beside a wall mark, with the coin below.
setup.caption: 2. Mark 2 metres on a wall. Hold the parachute with the coin hanging down, level with the mark, and let go.

setup.art: A child with a stopwatch and a parachute coming down, with arrows showing air pushing up on it.
setup.caption: 3. Time the fall three times, and then change one thing and time it again.

flow.do: Cut a square of plastic bag about 30 centimetres wide. Tape one piece of thread to each corner. Tie the other ends together around a coin. Mark 2 metres on a wall. Drop the plain coin three times and time each fall. Write the three times. A plain coin falls 2 metres in about 0.6 seconds.
flow.say: A plain coin falls fast. What do you think the parachute will change? Which force is the parachute meant to make bigger?
flow.kid: Time the plain coin falling 2 metres, three times.
flow.parent: Fold the parachute carefully before each drop and let go of the middle, so that the plastic opens in the air. A fall of 2 metres is short, so the time is short and your reaction matters. Do the drops three times, and use the middle.

flow.do: Drop the parachute from the same mark, and time three drops. If it falls in a spin or the plastic tangles, fix it and drop again. Write the times. Work out how many times longer the fall was than the plain coin's. Then think about why.
flow.say: The parachute takes longer to fall. What is the plastic doing to the air? Is the push of the air bigger or smaller?
flow.kid: Drop the parachute three times. Time each drop.

ask.q: Why is the parachute's time longer than the coin's?
good: The plastic gives the air a large surface to push against.
The push of the air upward grows until it nearly equals the weight, so the fall is slow.

flow.parent: A parachute catches a lot of air, so the push of the air upward is large for a small weight. The parachute reaches a slow steady speed. Expect about 1.5 to 2.5 seconds for 2 metres, about two to four times the plain coin's time. A very big canopy takes longer to open, so in a short fall it may not reach its steady speed.

flow.do: Change one thing at a time and test again, three drops each time. Try a bigger square or a smaller one. Try a hole in the middle the size of a coin. Try a different number of threads, or a lighter load. Write what you changed and the new time.
flow.say: What do you think will happen if you cut a small hole in the middle? Why might real parachutes have one?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test three drops. Write the time.

ask.q: What changed the fall time most?
good: The size of the plastic, because a larger parachute pushes more air.
Any change that gave the air more to push on made the fall slower.

flow.parent: A small hole at the top lets some air through and makes the fall steadier, because without it the parachute may swing from side to side. Real parachutes have a vent for this reason. A bigger square gives more air resistance and a slower fall. Changing two things at once makes it hard to know which one did the work.

flow.do: Compare your designs. Which gave the longest time? Draw the best one with arrows for the forces at its steady speed.
flow.say: At the steady speed, what two forces are balanced? Are the arrows the same length?
flow.kid: Draw your best parachute with two arrows.
flow.parent: At the slow steady speed, the weight down and the air's push up are equal. The parachute does not stop the Earth's pull. It makes the air's push big enough to match it at a small speed.
flow.think: Could a parachute work on the Moon, where there is no air? Why or why not?

general: Use a bigger square of plastic to catch more air.
Use more threads so that the parachute opens evenly.
creative: Cut a small hole at the middle so that the parachute swings less.
Use a round shape, a hexagon or a cone instead of a square.
Fold up the edges into small flaps to catch more air.
challenges.your_turn: Make a parachute with a shape of your own and test it. What helped the most? Is a slower fall always better?

challenges.title: A foil boat that carries the most coins
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge about upthrust. You fold a boat from a sheet of kitchen foil and see how many coins it can carry before it sinks.
challenges.problem: Make a boat from one square of kitchen foil, 20 centimetres on each side. It should carry the most coins in a bowl or bucket of water before it sinks. There is more than one good way to do it.
constraints: Use one square of foil, 20 by 20 centimetres, and nothing else for the boat.
Float the boat in a basin of water. Add coins one at a time, gently, to the middle.
Count the coins that the boat holds when it takes in water or tips over.
materials: kitchen foil, about 3 squares of 20 by 20 centimetres
a basin or bucket of water

setup.art: A square of foil turned into a shallow open boat, floating on water in a basin.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the edges of a foil square up to make a shallow tray and place it gently on the water.

setup.art: A foil boat low in the water with coins in the middle and a hand adding another.
setup.caption: 2. Put coins into the middle one at a time until the boat sinks or tips. Count them.

setup.art: Three foil boats side by side: a shallow tray, a deep tray and a boat with a pointed front.
setup.caption: 3. Change the shape and try again.

flow.do: Fold up each edge of a foil square about 2 centimetres to make a shallow tray. Float it in a basin of water on a table. Add coins one at a time, in the middle, until the boat takes in water or tips. Write the number. This is your first design.
flow.say: A square of foil sinks by itself. Why do you think it floats when it is folded into a tray?
flow.kid: Fold up the edges of the foil. Float it. Add coins one at a time.
flow.parent: The tray pushes aside more water than a flat foil, so the upthrust is greater. The boat floats until the water reaches the edge. After that, water pours in over the side. Expect between 20 and 80 coins, depending on the shape. If your first boat leaks, check for small holes in the foil.

flow.do: Try the usual solutions. Make the sides higher, about 4 centimetres. Make a long narrow boat or a wide flat one. Fold a double layer on the bottom. Test each design twice and write the numbers.
flow.say: Which do you think will carry the most coins: a deep boat, or a wide, shallow one? Why?
flow.kid: Make a boat with higher sides. Test it. Make a long narrow one. Test it.

ask.q: Why does a bigger boat carry more coins?
good: It pushes aside more water, so the upthrust is greater.
It can sink lower before water comes in.

flow.parent: A deeper, wider boat pushes aside more water before water spills in, so it carries more. A boat that is too tall and narrow may tip over. Coins in the middle keep the weight low and central.
