flow.do: Now try creative ideas. Put the coins at the bottom in a thin layer along the middle. Make a boat with a pointed front like a canoe. Fold a boat with a keel, which is a ridge along the bottom. Or make a boat that stays dry on the inside with a very tall edge. Test each, twice.
flow.say: Where do you think is the best place for the coins: in the middle or at the end? Why?
flow.kid: Make a boat with a pointed front. Put the coins in the middle. Test it.

ask.q: Why do the coins tip the boat when they are put on one side?
good: The weight on one side pulls that side down, and the boat can turn over.
The upthrust and the weight must act along the same line for the boat to stay level.

flow.parent: A low, central load makes the boat steadier. A pointed bow moves through water more easily but carries less than a wide boat of the same foil. There are many good answers.

flow.do: Compare your best boats. Which one carried the most coins? Draw the best boat with arrows for weight and upthrust. Dry the foil and the basin, and pour the water on a plant.
flow.say: At the moment before it sinks, what do you think is true of the weight and the upthrust?
flow.kid: Draw the best boat with two arrows. Dry up.
flow.parent: The weight of the boat and the coins equals the upthrust, which equals the weight of the water the boat pushes aside. At the moment of sinking, the boat can push aside no more water.
flow.think: Could you make a boat from the same foil that carries more than 100 coins? What would you need?

general: Make the boat wider so it pushes more water aside.
Place the coins low in the middle.
creative: Add a ridge along the bottom, like the keel of a boat.
Make a boat with two hulls joined across the top.
Fold a boat with a pointed front and a wide back.
challenges.your_turn: Make a boat of your own design from the foil. What did you change from your first boat, and how did it help? Do you think a boat could be too heavy to float?

worksheets.title: Finding forces on everyday things (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet practises the two questions that find forces on any thing, and the names and units of everyday forces.

items.p: A cup rests on a shelf. Show the forces on the cup.
items.obj: a cup resting on a shelf
items.why: The Earth pulls the cup down. The shelf touches the cup and pushes up. The cup is still, so the two are equal. There is no rope, so no tension, and the cup is not sliding, so no friction is needed.

items.p: A bag of sugar has a mass of 1 kilogram. About how hard does the Earth pull it?
opts: 10 newtons
1 newton
100 newtons
items.why: Each kilogram is pulled down by about 10 newtons. One newton is about the weight of a small apple, so a whole kilogram is about ten of them.

items.p: A child with a mass of 30 kilograms is pulled down by the Earth with roughly ____ newtons.
items.why: 30 × 10 = 300. Each kilogram is pulled by about 10 newtons.

items.p: The Earth pulls on a book on a table only while the book is falling.
items.why: False. The Earth pulls on the book all the time. On the table, the table pushes up as hard as the Earth pulls down, so the book stays still.

items.p: Sort each one by how the force reaches the thing.
items: the Earth's pull on a mango on a branch
Acts across a gap
a hook holding up a bag
Needs touching
a magnet pulling a steel pin through the air
Acts across a gap
the road gripping a chappal
Needs touching
a rubbed balloon pulling tiny paper bits
Acts across a gap
a table pushing up on a book
Needs touching
items.why: Gravity, magnetic force and the electric force reach across a gap. Tension, friction and the support force come from things that touch.

items.p: Match each force to a place where you meet it.
pairs: the strap holding a hanging bag
water holding up a floating katori
the grip of a chappal on a road
the push on a hand held out of a car window
items.why: Each force comes from a different kind of thing. A rope or strap gives tension, water gives upthrust, a rough surface gives friction, a solid surface gives support and moving air gives air resistance.

items.p: Put these steps for drawing a force diagram in order.
a: Pick one thing and draw it as a box
Ask what is pulling it from a distance
Draw one arrow for each force and label it
Check that arrows for balanced forces are the same length
items.why: You must choose the thing first, then find its forces, then draw them, then check. Skipping the question about the pull from far is how the Earth's pull gets forgotten.

items.p: A friend says, 'A book on a table has no force on it, because it is still.' What would you say?
items.a: The book has two forces: the Earth pulls it down and the table pushes it up. They are equal, so they balance and the book does not move. Not moving does not mean no force. A good answer names both forces and says they are equal.
items.why: A strong answer names the weight and the support force, says they are equal and gives the reason why the book stays still.

items.p: Draw a force diagram for a bucket hanging still from a rope in a well. Label each arrow.
items.a: A box or bucket with one arrow up labelled 'rope pulls (tension)' and one arrow down labelled 'the Earth pulls (weight)', the same length.
items.why: The bucket is still, so the two arrows cancel. The rope is touching it and pulls up. The Earth pulls down from a distance.
items.art: A blank space with a small bucket at the middle and room for arrows.

items.p: Is a book on a table 'doing nothing'?

views.says: Things stay together through opposite pulls, as a bow keeps its shape. The book rests because two pulls match.

views.who: A physicist who thinks of forces as numbers that add up
views.says: The forces are only numbers that add to zero. Nothing is 'holding' or 'keeping' anything.

items.ask: Which way of speaking would you use for the book? Could both be useful?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says both descriptions give the same prediction. The first stresses what is going on, and the second stresses what can be calculated.
items.why: Both views agree that the forces add to zero. They differ on whether the words 'holding' and 'keeping' describe something that is going on. No view is marked right.

items.p: A coin and a flat sheet of paper are dropped. The coin lands first. Which is the best reason?
opts: Air pushes back much harder on the sheet for its weight
Gravity does not pull on paper
Heavy things always fall faster, even without air
items.why: The sheet has a big area for its weight, so the push of the air balances its weight at a low speed. Gravity pulls on both. Without air they would land together.

items.p: In a tug of war, nobody moves. The red team pulls with 1,500 newtons. How hard does the blue team pull?
items.why: The rope is not moving, so the forces on it are balanced. The blue team must pull with 1,500 newtons as well.

items.p: A magnet pulls a steel pin, a wooden pencil and a copper coin with equal force.
items.why: False. A magnet pulls strongly on iron and steel, and on a few other materials such as nickel and cobalt. It hardly pulls wood or copper.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Gravity, magnetic force, tension, electric force.
items.a: Tension, because it needs a tight rope in contact. The other three act across a gap.
items.why: Gravity, magnetic force and the electric force can pull on a thing that is not touching them. A rope's tension acts only through the rope itself.

items.p: The biceps is a muscle in the upper arm. Which is true of every muscle?
opts: It can only pull
It can push and pull
It can only push
items.why: A muscle shortens, and so pulls on what it is joined to. The arm needs one muscle to bend it and another to straighten it.

items.p: Label the forces on a kite held steady in the sky.
a: pull of the string: down and towards the flier, along the string
weight of the kite: straight down
push of the wind: up and away from the flier, against the kite
items.art: A diamond-shaped kite in the sky with a string leading down to the ground and three empty label lines.
items.why: The kite is held steady, so the three forces balance. The string and the weight both pull partly downward, and the wind pushes up and away from the flier to cancel them.

worksheets.title: Muscles, levers and the push of the air (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet goes a step further. It uses numbers for levers and for falling, and compares two ways of describing a force.

items.p: A 20 newton load hangs 30 centimetres from a pivot. A muscle joins 5 centimetres from it. How hard must it pull?
opts: 4 newtons
20 newtons
120 newtons
items.why: The muscle must make as much turning effect as the load. Load times distance is 20 × 30 = 600. The muscle's distance is 5, so its pull is 600 ÷ 5 = 120 newtons.

items.p: A 20 kilogram child sits 2 metres from a see-saw's middle. How far out must a 10 kilogram child sit?
items.why: Weight times distance must match on both sides. 20 × 2 = 40, and 10 × 4 = 40.

items.p: A 2 kilogram bag of rice hangs from a string. The tension in the string is about ____ newtons.
items.why: 2 × 10 = 20 newtons. The string must pull up exactly as hard as the Earth pulls down.

items.p: In a tug of war where neither team moves, neither team is pulling.
items.why: False. Each team may be pulling with thousands of newtons. The pulls are equal and opposite, so the rope does not move.

items.p: Sort each force by how it behaves when the thing goes faster.
cats: Stays the same at any speed
items: the air's push on a cyclist
Grows as the speed grows
the weight of a school bag
Stays the same at any speed
the water's push on a person wading through a pool
Grows as the speed grows
the upthrust on a floating katori
Stays the same at any speed
the Earth's pull on a falling cone
Stays the same at any speed
items.why: Air and water push back harder the faster you push through them. Weight and the upthrust on a floating thing depend on the thing and the water, not on speed.

items.p: Put these in order of steady falling speed, from slowest to fastest.
a: a paper cone, about 5 kilometres per hour
a skydiver under an open parachute, about 20 kilometres per hour
a large raindrop, about 32 kilometres per hour
a skydiver lying flat, about 200 kilometres per hour
items.why: The more air a falling thing has to push against for its weight, the slower its steady speed. A cone is wide and light. A skydiver lying flat is heavy for the area and falls fastest.

items.p: Match each still or steady thing to its pair of balanced forces.
pairs: a bucket rising steadily from a well
a cyclist at a steady speed
items.why: A thing that is still or at a steady speed has its forces in balanced pairs. Each pair comes from what is touching the thing or pulling it from far.

items.p: Four cones fell far less than four times as fast as one. A friend expected four times as fast. Explain the mistake.
items.a: The friend forgets the push of the air. A cone stops speeding up when the push of the air equals its weight. The push grows faster than the speed: twice the speed gives about four times the push. So four times the weight is matched at about twice the speed.
items.why: A strong answer says the push of the air grows faster than the speed, and uses the idea of a steady speed.

items.p: Draw a force diagram for a cone just let go. Draw another at its steady speed. How do the arrows differ?
items.a: Just after letting go: a long arrow down for weight and a very short arrow up for air resistance. At the steady speed: two arrows of equal length, one down and one up.
items.why: At first the air pushes very little, so weight wins and the cone speeds up. As it goes faster, the air's arrow grows until it matches the weight.
items.art: Two blank boxes side by side, each with a small paper cone in the middle.

items.p: Gravity: a pull, or a bend in space and time?

views.says: Gravity is a force that pulls every mass towards every other. His rule gives how strong the pull is, and he wrote that he would make no guess about the cause.
A mass bends the space and time around it. A falling ball has no force on it and simply follows the bend.

items.ask: Which would you use to work out when a dropped ball lands? Which would you use for satellite navigation? Does it matter?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says both predict an everyday fall equally well, and that Einstein's picture is needed for the very exact timing in satellite navigation. No view is marked right, because physicists use both and have no theory that joins gravity with tiny particles.
items.why: Newton's rule is a very good description for everyday life. Einstein's gives better answers in extreme cases. Neither says what gravity finally is.

items.p: A magnet stays on a fridge door and does not slide down. Which force holds it up?
opts: The magnetic pull, which points up
Gravity, which points up near a magnet
Friction between the magnet and the door
items.why: The magnet's pull points into the door, not up. That pull presses the magnet to the door, and the grip of friction along the door holds the magnet up against its weight.

items.p: Which force is behind the push of a table on a book?
opts: The electromagnetic force between atoms
Gravity between the table and the book
A force inside the centres of atoms
items.why: The atoms of the table and the book push on each other electrically. Gravity between a table and a book is far too weak to matter.

items.p: A grown-up with a mass of 45 kilograms stands still. How many newtons does the floor push up with?
items.why: The grown-up is still, so the floor pushes up exactly as hard as the Earth pulls down: 45 × 10 = 450 newtons.

items.p: Which is not in balance? A resting book, a ball at the top of a throw, a hanging lamp, a steady cyclist.
items.a: The ball at the top of its throw, because only its weight is pulling it and nothing cancels that.
items.why: The other three have forces that cancel. The ball is not moving for an instant but is about to fall, so its forces are not in balance.

items.p: A strong muscle can push a bone.
items.why: False. A muscle can only pull. A bone is pushed when a muscle on the other side of the joint pulls.

items.p: Label this drawing of an arm holding a bottle: the pivot, where the biceps joins, and the bottle.
a: where the biceps joins: about 4 centimetres from the elbow, on the forearm
bottle: about 30 centimetres from the elbow, in the hand
items.art: A side view of a bent arm with the elbow at the left, a short mark on the forearm near the elbow and a bottle in the hand, with three empty label lines.
items.why: The bottle is far from the pivot and the muscle joins near it. That is why the muscle has to pull many times harder than the bottle weighs.

worksheets.title: Faulty reasoning and open questions about forces (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet tests reasoning. You spot faults in claims, use numbers on levers and ropes, and think about questions that scientists have not settled.

items.p: An astronaut says, 'There is no gravity in my station, because I float.' What is wrong?
opts: Nothing. Floating shows gravity is zero
The station is too heavy to be pulled
Gravity is strong there. She floats because she falls with the station
items.why: At 400 kilometres, gravity is still about nine-tenths of the ground value. Floating means no floor is pushing on her, not that nothing is pulling her.

items.p: A scale under your feet in a lift that is falling freely would read zero.
items.why: True. The lift and you fall together, so the floor does not push on you. The scale measures that push, not the Earth's pull.

items.p: A 10 newton bottle is 32 centimetres from the elbow. The biceps joins 4 centimetres away. It pulls about ____ newtons.
items.why: 10 × 32 = 320, and 320 ÷ 4 = 80. The muscle pulls about 8 times the load.

items.p: A 15 newton load is 36 centimetres from the elbow. The muscle joins 4 centimetres away. How hard does it pull?
Two people pull opposite ends of a rope with 100 newtons each. The rope stays still. What is the tension?
opts: 200 newtons
0 newtons
100 newtons
items.why: The rope is pulled with 100 newtons at each end, and carries 100 newtons along its length. The two pulls do not add up to the tension. If you chose 200, imagine tying one end to a wall: the pull is still 100 newtons.

items.p: Nobody has ever seen a force. What do we see, and what do we say a force did?
items.a: We see a spring stretch, a ball speed up, a book stay still or a rope tighten. We say that a force did it. A force is a name for what changes motion or shape, and we measure it from what happens.
items.why: A strong answer separates what is seen from the word 'force'. It says that force is a working idea, and that scientists do not all agree it is basic.

items.p: A heavier skydiver falls faster than a lighter one under the same kind of parachute. Use forces to explain why.
items.a: The heavier skydiver has a greater weight, so the push of the air must grow bigger to match it. The push grows with speed, so the steady speed is higher.
items.why: A strong answer says the steady speed is the one at which the air's push equals the weight. A bigger weight needs a bigger push, and so a faster fall.

items.p: A skydiver spreads her arms and legs wide. What happens to the steady falling speed?
opts: It gets higher, because she is bigger
It stays the same, because her weight is the same
It gets lower, because the air has more to push on
items.why: The same weight is now met by the air's push at a lower speed, because there is more area to push on. Many skydivers use this to slow down.

items.p: When a root turns downward in the cup, is the root deciding or being moved?

views.who: Plant behaviour researchers such as Stefano Mancuso
views.says: A root tip senses gravity, water, touch and light together, and then chooses where to grow. That is a kind of thinking.

views.who: Plant physiologists who call this a tropism
views.says: A tropism is a built-in response. Cells in the root sense gravity and growth chemicals make one side grow faster, with no choosing.

items.ask: Which description do you find more convincing? What could you test to tell them apart?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says the facts seen in the cup are the same under both descriptions. It also suggests a test, such as putting water on one side while gravity points the other way. No view is marked right.
items.why: Both agree that the root senses gravity and that its turn is not random. They differ on whether the word 'deciding' fits, which is a question about thinking and not about the measurements.

items.p: Draw the forces on a person leaning on a wall with straight arms, not slipping. Use four arrows.
items.a: A person leaning at a slant, with weight down and a floor push up. Friction from the floor points towards the wall, and the wall pushes back away from the wall. Up equals down, and the two sideways forces are equal.
items.why: The person is still, so each pair of forces cancels. Friction from the floor must hold the feet from sliding away from the wall.
items.art: A blank space with a stick person leaning against a wall, hands on the wall, feet on the floor.

items.p: Sort each force by what lies underneath it.
items: the grip of a chappal on a road
The electromagnetic force between atoms
the pull of the Earth on a mango
Gravity
a magnet pulling a pin
The electromagnetic force between atoms
a muscle pulling on a bone
The electromagnetic force between atoms
a satellite held in orbit
Gravity
items.why: Pushes by surfaces and ropes, the magnet's pull and the muscle's pull all come from electric and magnetic forces between atoms. The pull of the Earth on a mango and on a satellite is gravity.

items.p: Match each odd observation to the force that explains it.
pairs: a steel katori floats when set down gently
a root turns down in a cup on its side
the pull of the Earth, sensed by the root
a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall
a fridge magnet holds a paper in place
items.why: Each observation points to a force that a diagram would show. A force explains a change or a balance.

items.p: Newton's rule and Einstein's picture of gravity predict the same fall of a ball. What does this tell us?
opts: A description can work very well without being the last word
Newton was wrong, so his rule is useless
Einstein must be wrong, because Newton's rule is simpler
items.why: Two different pictures can give the same prediction. Scientists keep both, and keep asking what gravity finally is.

items.p: A 50 newton box slides at a steady speed under a 15 newton push. How many newtons of friction act on it?
items.why: At a steady speed the forces along the floor are balanced, so friction equals the push, which is 15 newtons.

items.p: How could you show that water pushes up on a stone, when the stone sinks?
items.a: Lift the stone on a string with a spring or a rubber band. Note how far the band stretches in air. Lower the stone into water and see the band shorten. The stone seems lighter because the water pushes up on it.
items.why: A strong answer lowers the stone on something that measures weight, such as a rubber band, and compares the reading in air and in water.

quiz.p: A lamp hangs still from a chain. Which forces act on the lamp?
opts: Only the Earth pulls, because the lamp is not moving
The chain pulls up and nothing pulls down
The chain pulls up and the Earth pulls down
A force pushes it down from the ceiling
quiz.why: Pick one thing and ask what touches it and what pulls it from far. The chain touches it and pulls up. The Earth pulls down from a distance. If you chose only gravity, you forgot that a still thing needs an upward force from something touching it.

quiz.p: Which is true of a rope or a string?
opts: It can push and pull equally well
It pulls only when it hangs loose
It can pull, but it cannot push
It pushes when it is wet
quiz.why: A rope pulls along its length when it is tight, and a slack rope does nothing. If you chose pushing, try pushing a thread across a table: it just folds.

quiz.p: Astronauts in a station 400 kilometres up float. What is the reason?
opts: There is no gravity so high up
They fall with the station, so no floor pushes on them
The station's walls block the Earth's pull
They are too far from the Earth to be pulled at all
quiz.why: At that height gravity is still about nine-tenths as strong as in your room. They float because they and the station fall together and the floor does not push on their feet. Choosing 'no gravity' mixes up a missing push with a missing pull.

quiz.p: A steel katori floats, but a steel spoon sinks. Which is the best reason?
opts: The steel in a katori weighs less than steel in a spoon
Water pushes up only on bowls
A spoon is too small for water to push on
Its hollow shape pushes aside enough water to hold it up
quiz.why: Upthrust equals the weight of the water pushed aside. A hollow shape pushes aside a lot of water and a lump of steel does not. If you chose 'weighs less', try weighing both: the steel itself is the same.

quiz.p: A bag of rice hangs still. The string pulls up with 20 newtons. How hard does the Earth pull down?
opts: 20 newtons
10 newtons
0 newtons, because the bag is not moving
quiz.why: The bag is still, so the forces are balanced and the down pull must equal the up pull, which is 20 newtons. Choosing 0 treats 'not moving' as 'no force'. Choosing 10 has no reason behind it.

quiz.p: A cyclist keeps a steady speed on a flat road. What is true of the forces along the road?
opts: Forward force equals backward force, so her speed stays the same
The forward force must be bigger, or she would stop
No force acts on her, because the speed is steady
quiz.why: Balanced forces mean no change in speed, and a steady speed is a kind of 'no change'. A bigger forward force would make her speed up. A cycle slows after you stop pedalling because friction and air still push backward.

quiz.p: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top, it is not moving for an instant. Is a force on it?
opts: No, a still thing has no force on it
Yes. Gravity still pulls it down, and it starts to fall
Yes, the push of the throw is still on it
quiz.why: Gravity never switches off. At the top, the ball's speed is zero for an instant, and the pull down is not balanced, so it speeds up downward. If you chose the push of the throw, that push ended when the ball left the hand.

quiz.p: Which force diagram shows a book resting on a table?
opts: One long arrow down only
One arrow up only
Two arrows of the same length, one down and one up
A long arrow down and a short arrow up
quiz.why: The book is still, so the arrows must cancel. The weight down and the support force up are equal. A long arrow down with a short one up would show a book that is sinking through the table.

quiz.p: What does a force diagram of a kite show?
opts: The kite and the person, with arrows for both
The kite alone, with one arrow for each force on it
One arrow for the biggest force only
quiz.why: A force diagram draws one thing alone, so you can see everything that pushes or pulls it. Drawing the person too mixes up forces on different things. Drawing only the biggest force hides the ones that balance it.

quiz.p: Four paper cones pressed together fall far less than four times as fast as one cone. Why?
opts: Cones cannot fall faster than one cone
The air pushes four times harder on the stack at any speed
Gravity pulls the stack only twice as hard
The air's push grows faster than the speed, so twice the speed is enough
quiz.why: A thing stops speeding up when the push of the air equals its weight. Double the speed gives about four times the push, so four times the weight is matched at about twice the speed. If you chose gravity, remember that four cones are pulled four times as hard.

quiz.p: In a room with air, a hammer beats a feather to the floor. What happens with no air?
opts: The hammer would still land first because it is heavier
The feather would land first because it is lighter
They would land together
quiz.why: The feather is held back by the push of the air, which is big for its weight. With no air there is only gravity, and everything falls at the same rate. On the Moon in 1971 the astronaut David Scott showed this.

quiz.p: A large raindrop keeps speeding up all the way down from the cloud.
quiz.why: False. The push of the air grows as the drop speeds up, until it equals the drop's weight. Then the drop falls at a steady speed of about 9 metres each second.

quiz.p: Why does your biceps pull about 8 times as hard as the bottle weighs?
opts: It is about 8 times stronger than other muscles
A muscle pushes as well as pulls, so it does double work
Pulling up always takes eight times the force
It joins close to the elbow, but the bottle is far away
quiz.why: The forearm is a lever with the elbow as its pivot. A pull close to the pivot must be much bigger to balance a load far from it. The muscle is not special, but its position gives it a big job.

quiz.p: Which of these is, underneath, the same force as a magnet's pull?
opts: The pull of the Earth on a mango
The pull of the Sun on the Earth
Nothing is the same as a magnet's pull
The grip of a chappal on the road
quiz.why: Friction, tension, the push of a table and a muscle's pull all come from the electromagnetic force between atoms. That force also gives a magnet's pull. Gravity is a separate force.

quiz.p: Which of these does nobody yet know?
opts: Whether gravity can be joined with the physics of tiny particles
How hard the Earth pulls a 1 kilogram bag
Whether a magnet pulls steel
Whether a table pushes up on a book
quiz.why: Scientists can predict gravity's effects very exactly but have no agreed account that joins gravity with the physics of tiny particles. The other three are measured and agreed.

applications: The large shore nets at Fort Kochi in Kerala are tipped like a see-saw. Stones hung on ropes at the back balance the weight of the wet net at the front. A small crew can lift a net wider than a room, because the lever works for them. Look at the picture in the lesson, then look at a see-saw in a park.

A lift cabin hangs from steel cables. Each cable carries tension equal to part of the weight of the cabin and the people inside. Lifts have many cables, so that if one failed the others would still hold. If you travel in a lift, look at the sign that gives the greatest load in kilograms.

A shop's old balance scale, the tarazu, is a lever with equal arms. A kilogram weight on one pan is balanced by 1 kilogram of rice on the other, because they are at equal distances from the middle. A parent can look at one in a local shop and ask how it would change if the arms were unequal.

Shoes, tyres and cricket bats are made with grooves, patterns or rough rubber. These raise friction so that the shoe grips the ground and the tyre grips the road. The tyres of a bus have deep grooves that push water away so that the rubber, not a film of water, meets the road.

A life jacket and a ship's hull work through upthrust. A hollow hull pushes aside a huge weight of water. Ships have a painted line on the side, the load line, which shows how low they may sit in the water. Look for it on a picture of a ship.

A compass needle turns because the Earth is a huge, weak magnet. Sailors used it for navigation for many centuries. About 1088 CE the Chinese scholar Shen Kuo described a magnetised needle that points a little off true north, which is why compasses need correcting.

A tower crane at a building site has a long arm in front and heavy concrete blocks at the back. The blocks balance the load, as the stones balance the net at Fort Kochi. Look for the blocks when you pass a building site.

spotted.text: Stand in a bus holding the handrail, and look at a hanging strap. When the bus pulls away, the strap swings back. When the bus brakes, it swings forward. Notice that when the bus moves steadily, the strap hangs straight down, which shows that its forces are balanced.
spotted.art: A bus interior with a hanging strap drawn in three positions: leaning back, straight and leaning forward.

spotted.text: Next time you stop pedalling a cycle on a flat lane, count how many seconds it takes to slow right down. Notice that you slow down even though nobody is pushing against you. Friction and the air are pushing backward all the time.
spotted.art: A child on a cycle freewheeling along a village lane, with a small backward arrow on the wheel.

spotted.text: Pull a fridge door slowly open. At the edge, feel a small tug. A magnetic strip in the rubber seal is pulling the door to the fridge across the last bit of gap. Notice that it pulls harder the closer the door comes.
spotted.art: A fridge door opened a finger-width with a dotted line along the rubber seal and a tiny arrow pulling inward.

spotted.text: At a bathroom door, watch how your feet grip when the floor is dry and when it is wet. On the wet floor, your foot slides back. Notice that friction is what pushes you forward when you walk.
spotted.art: A pair of bare feet on a wet tile with a small curved arrow showing the slide.

spotted.text: When it rains, drop a leaf, a coin and a small steel spoon into a puddle or a bucket. Notice which float and which sink. Then push the floating leaf under the water with a finger and feel it push back.
spotted.art: A bucket of rain water with a leaf floating, a coin and a spoon at the bottom, and a finger pushing the leaf down.

spotted.text: Look at an electricity wire strung between two poles on your street. Notice that it sags in a smooth curve, never in a straight line. The wire pulls on both poles along its length, and its weight pulls it down. That pull is tension.
spotted.art: Two electric poles with a wire sagging between them and arrows pulling in along the wire at each pole.

spotted.text: At a playground, watch a swing at its lowest point. Notice that the chains are pulling hardest there, and that the swing is moving fastest. Then look at the highest point where it stops for an instant.
spotted.art: A swing seen from the side drawn at the top and bottom of its path, with arrows along the chains.

spotted.text: If a potted plant has been knocked over, check the plant after two or three days. Notice that the new shoot at the top has turned upward, away from the pull of the Earth. The plant is sensing which way is down.
spotted.art: A pot lying on its side, with a shoot curving upward at the open end.

ask_kids: You hold a school bag out in front of you and your arm gets tired. The bag is not moving. What is your arm doing?
If the Earth pulls you down, and you pull the Earth up just as hard, why does only one of you move?
A floating leaf, a floating katori and a big ship are all held up by water. What do they have in common?
Why does a heavy raindrop not hurt when it falls from a high cloud?
A fridge magnet does not touch the paper clip, and it still moves it. What is reaching across the gap?
Which is harder: pushing a door near the hinge or near the handle? Why do you think so?
Think of a bridge you know. Where do the pushes and pulls of a bus on it finally go?
Nobody has ever seen a force. Do you think a force is real, or a way of talking? What would you test?

maths.problem: A bag of 3 kilograms of rice is weighed on the Earth. On the Moon, the pull is about one sixth as strong. Find the weight of the bag in newtons on the Earth and on the Moon, and the mass of the bag on each.
maths.answer: 30 newtons on the Earth, 5 newtons on the Moon. The mass is 3 kilograms on both.
maths.explain: On the Earth: 3 × 10 = 30 newtons. On the Moon: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 newtons. The rice is the same stuff, so its mass stays 3 kilograms.
maths.context: This problem uses the idea from the scale test that weight is a pull measured in newtons, and mass is how much stuff there is.
maths.why_maths: Weight changes with the pull of the world the thing is on, while mass does not. The sums are multiplying by 10 and dividing by 6, which is the maths physicists use to compare worlds.

maths.problem: At the cone's steady speed of 1.4 metres per second, the air's push equals the cone's weight, 0.016 newtons. The push grows as the square of the speed. How big would the push be at 2.8 metres per second, which is twice the speed? How big at 4.2 metres per second?
maths.answer: 0.064 newtons at 2.8 metres per second, and 0.144 newtons at 4.2 metres per second.
maths.explain: Twice the speed: 2 × 2 = 4 times the push, 0.016 × 4 = 0.064. Three times the speed: 3 × 3 = 9 times the push, 0.016 × 9 = 0.144.
maths.context: This problem works out the push of the air at different speeds for a cone that steadily falls.
maths.why_maths: Squaring explains why four stacked cones fall only twice as fast as one. A push that grows with the square of the speed becomes four times as large when the speed doubles. So the cone needs only twice the speed to match four times the weight.

maths.problem: A ruler rests on a pencil at its 15 centimetre mark. Three coins sit 5 centimetres from the pivot on the left. One coin sits on the right. Where must it sit to balance? Use the rule: number of coins times distance is equal on both sides.
maths.answer: 15 centimetres from the pivot, at the very end of the ruler.
maths.explain: Left side: 3 × 5 = 15. The right side must also be 15, so 1 coin × distance = 15, and the distance is 15 centimetres.
maths.context: This problem uses the balance rule from the coin see-saw.
maths.why_maths: A lever balances when the products on both sides are equal, so finding a missing number is solving a balance, exactly the maths of the lever.

maths.problem: A steel katori pushes aside 150 millilitres of water when it is full to the brim without sinking. One millilitre of water weighs about 0.01 newtons, and the katori weighs 0.7 newtons. How many 1 rupee coins, each weighing about 0.04 newtons (about 4 grams, which differs a little between coin series), can it carry before it sinks?
maths.explain: The most upthrust is 150 × 0.01 = 1.5 newtons. The katori itself uses 0.7, so 1.5 − 0.7 = 0.8 newtons is left for coins. 0.8 ÷ 0.04 = 20 coins.
maths.context: This problem works out how many coins the katori in the floating activity should carry. It uses the rule that upthrust equals the weight of the water pushed aside.
maths.why_maths: It turns the idea of upthrust into a sum a family can check by testing. It also shows that the answer depends on the size of the katori.

maths.problem: A bottle of 10 newtons is 32 centimetres from the elbow. The biceps joins the forearm 4 centimetres from the elbow. How many times bigger is the biceps pull than the load, and how big is it? Then say what happens to the pull if the muscle joined 8 centimetres from the elbow.
maths.answer: 8 times, so 80 newtons. At 8 centimetres it would be 4 times, so 40 newtons.
maths.explain: The load's distance is 32 and the muscle's is 4. 32 ÷ 4 = 8, so the muscle pulls 8 × 10 = 80 newtons. At 8 centimetres: 32 ÷ 8 = 4, and 4 × 10 = 40. Halving the distance doubles the pull.
maths.context: This problem uses the numbers from the arm-lever activity.
maths.why_maths: It is a ratio problem. The pull is the load times the ratio of the two distances, and a smaller distance means a larger pull. This is why the arrangement of the body costs the muscle a lot.

maths.problem: On the International Space Station, the pull of the Earth is about 9 tenths of its value on the ground. A child of 30 kilograms is pulled down with 300 newtons on the ground. How big is the pull on the child on the station? Why does the child float anyway?
maths.answer: 270 newtons, near enough. The child floats because the station and the child fall together, so no floor pushes up on them.
maths.explain: 9 tenths of 300 is 300 ÷ 10 × 9 = 270 newtons. The pull is almost as strong as on the ground. What is missing is the push of a floor.
maths.context: This problem works out the Earth's pull at the height of the space station and asks what makes a floating astronaut weightless.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of a quantity gives the weaker pull. The answer, 270, is almost as big as 300, and this surprising result says that weightlessness is not the lack of gravity.

maths.problem: In three drops of one paper cone from 2 metres, the times are 1.5, 1.3 and 1.6 seconds. Find the middle time and the average, and the speed over 2 metres using the middle time. Then say why we use the middle and not the biggest.
maths.answer: The middle time is 1.5 seconds and the average is 1.47 seconds. The speed is about 1.3 metres per second. A drop that goes wrong is often the biggest or smallest, and the middle is not pulled by it.
maths.explain: The middle of 1.3, 1.5 and 1.6 is 1.5. The average is (1.5 + 1.3 + 1.6) ÷ 3 = 4.4 ÷ 3 = 1.47. The speed is 2 ÷ 1.5 = 1.33 metres per second.
maths.context: This problem uses made-up results of the falling cone test to compare the middle time with the average.
maths.why_maths: A stopwatch held by a hand is never exact. The middle value is a fair way to describe three tries, because one bad drop cannot pull it far.

quiz: A book on a table has no force on it, because it is not moving.
The Earth pulls it down and the table pushes it up. The forces are equal, so the book does not move.
The Earth pulls on you even when you are sitting still.
Gravity never switches off. The chair pushes up as hard as the Earth pulls down.
A rope can push things if it is thick enough.
A rope can only pull. A thick rope is stronger, but it still folds when pushed.
Astronauts on the space station float because there is no gravity there.
Gravity there is about nine-tenths as strong as on the ground. They float because they are falling together with the station.
A steel katori can float on water.
Its hollow shape pushes aside enough water to give an upthrust equal to its weight.
A muscle can pull and push.
A muscle can only pull. A second muscle on the other side of the joint pulls the other way.
A magnet pulls on copper as strongly as on iron.
A magnet pulls strongly on iron and steel, but hardly at all on copper.
A falling raindrop speeds up until the push of the air equals its weight.
Then it falls at a steady speed of about 9 metres each second for a large drop.
Friction can push you forward when you walk.
Your foot pushes backward on the ground, and the friction on your foot points forward.
Gravity and the magnetic force are the same force.
Physicists know of gravity and the electromagnetic force as separate forces. Magnetic force is part of the electromagnetic force.
odd: Tension, upthrust and friction all come from things that touch the object. Gravity pulls across a gap.
A magnet, a charged balloon and the Earth all pull across a gap. A rope pulls only by touching.
A biceps, a heart and a triceps are all muscles that pull. Ice is not.
A newton measures force. A metre, a kilogram and a second measure length, mass and time.
